title: Install
text:
Installing barRoso
The barRoso package is available on GitHub and can be installed using devtools. Before installation, make sure you have the following packages installed:

devtools
LCVP
lcvplants

# Install devtools if needed
install.packages("devtools")

# Install dependencies
devtools::install_github("idiv-biodiversity/LCVP")
devtools::install_github("idiv-biodiversity/lcvplants")

# Install barRoso
devtools::install_github("DBOSlab/barRoso")

title: Install
text:
Load the package
library(barRoso)
You are now ready to start cleaning, standardizing, and analyzing plant specimen records.

title: barroso_fix_names
text:
barRoso::barroso_fix_names()


Description
Updates misspelled names and synonyms of herbarium records into accepted names, using the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) of Plants of the World Online as a global backbone, through the package expowo, and by default the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB), through the package floraR. It is meant to be run after barroso_cat() and before barroso_std(), so that duplicates identified with synonyms or misspelled names are recognized.


Details
Each unique binomial built from genus and specificEpithet is searched just once, so large datasets (e.g. all records of REFLORA and JABOT) are harmonized quickly. Names without a specific epithet (e.g. "Ormosia", "Ormosia sp.") are not searched.

WCVP: all names of the families in the data (and, with flora_brasil = TRUE, the families of their genera in FFB) are read at once with expowo::powoSpecies(family, synonyms = TRUE), from the WCVP kept in the cache of expowo. Names are first matched exactly; misspelled names are matched to the closest name of the same genus, with a relative distance of the specific epithet up to max_distance (e.g. "Ormosia fastigiatta" to "Ormosia fastigiata"). Misspelled genera are matched in the same way. Homonyms with different accepted names (and ties between misspelled names) are left as they are, as "ambiguous".
FFB (flora_brasil = TRUE): the names are searched at once with floraR::flora_search(), which also corrects misspellings of the specific epithet. Names found in FFB follow FFB, which is preferred for the Brazilian flora, while the other names follow WCVP. A misspelling found in FFB is not taken for a name found as it is in WCVP, as names of other countries are often close to Brazilian names (e.g. "Ormosia panamensis" and "Ormosia paraensis"). The FFB dataset is downloaded once into the barRoso cache folder.

Accepted infraspecific names are reduced to the binomial (e.g. "Ormosia nobilis var. bolivarensis" as a synonym of "Ormosia bolivarensis"). When a name is updated, family, genus, specificEpithet, and when present species, scientificName, scientificNameAuthorship and taxonName, get the accepted name, and infraspecificEpithet becomes NA. The family is also updated for accepted names in another family (e.g. "Leguminosae" into "Fabaceae").
Three columns are added after specificEpithet:

taxonOriginal: the binomial (or genus) before the harmonization.
taxonStatus: "accepted", "synonym", "misspelled" (the misspelled name of an accepted name), "misspelled synonym", "ambiguous", "not found", or NA for names without specific epithet.
taxonSource: "FFB" or "WCVP".

The first use downloads the WCVP (by expowo) and the FFB dataset (by floraR), which are then kept in cache folders for the next uses.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame with herbarium records, e.g. from barroso_cat().


flora_brasil
Logical; if TRUE, names found in the Flora e Funga do Brasil follow FFB, and the other names follow WCVP. If FALSE, all names follow WCVP (default: TRUE).


max_distance
Maximum relative distance (0 to 1) between a misspelled name and an accepted or synonym name (default: 0.2).


vascular_only
Logical; if TRUE, records of families that are not in WCVP, which has only vascular plants (e.g. mosses, fungi and algae), and records without family are removed (default: FALSE).


colname_family
Column name for the family (default: "family").


colname_genus
Column name for the genus (default: "genus").


colname_specificEpithet
Column name for the specific epithet (default: "specificEpithet"). When missing, the epithet is taken from a binomial in the column species, as in GBIF downloads.


verbose
Logical; if TRUE, prints messages about the progress and a summary (default: TRUE).





Value
The data frame with accepted names and the columns taxonOriginal, taxonStatus and taxonSource.


Examples
data_all <- barroso_cat(list(REFLORA = data_reflora, JABOT = data_jabot),
                        keep_source = c("JABOT", "REFLORA"))
data_all <- barroso_fix_names(data_all, vascular_only = TRUE)
table(data_all$taxonStatus)
data_all <- barroso_std(data_all)

title: barroso_chars_template
text:
barRoso::barroso_chars_template()


Description
Given a data.frame of species (one row per species, or per specimen) OR a path to an Excel file containing such data, this function writes an .xlsx file whose columns begin with whatever identification columns are in species_df — Genus/Species/Author, Family/Taxon, etc. — and continue with a standard morphological-character template (HABIT, STIPULE, LEAF, INFLORESCENCE, FLOWER, FRUIT, SEED) left empty for the user to fill in.
When plant_group is specified, INFLORESCENCE/FLOWER/FRUIT blocks are replaced with the morphology that group actually has — e.g. Leguminosae-Papilionoideae swaps generic petals for STANDARD / WING / KEEL and adds stamen arrangement and fruit dehiscence; Asteraceae replaces the inflorescence with capitulum + involucre and the flower block with RAY / DISC florets + pappus; Ochnaceae uses the full carpophore/mericarp fruit and seed-apical-hook block; Myristicaceae has one sentence for each organ (Petiole, Leaf blade, Staminate and Pistillate inflorescences, Androecium, Ovary, Infructescence), with the exudate, the leaf trichomes, the anthers and the aril; Orchidaceae uses dorsal/lateral sepals, labellum and column. Supported groups:

“Leguminosae-Papilionoideae”
“Leguminosae-Caesalpinioideae”
“Leguminosae-Mimosoideae”
“Asteraceae”
“Myristicaceae”
“Ochnaceae”
“Orchidaceae”

The resulting file is the input format expected by barroso_write_descriptions(): column-name conventions match (capitalised group prefixes, lowercase subterms, “(cm)” / “(mm)” / “(m)” units, “length” / “width” / “height” keywords).


Arguments







Argument
Description




species_df
Either a data.frame containing the species-identification columns you want preserved (e.g. Genus, Species, Author), OR a character string path to an Excel file (.xlsx) containing such data. Every column in species_df is copied into the output as-is; template columns are appended after them and written empty. Any template column whose name already exists in species_df is skipped, so user data is never overwritten.


sheet
Character string or integer. Sheet name or index to read when species_df is a path to an Excel file. Default is 1.


plant_group
Optional character. One of the supported profiles listed above. NULL (default) uses the generic flowering-plant profile.


species_cols
Character vector or integer indices. Column names or indices used to build the species header (e.g., c(“Genus”, “Species”, “Author”) or 1:3). These can be combined flexibly (e.g., a single “Scientific_name” column or separate Genus, Species, and Author columns).


overwrite
Logical. If TRUE (default), an existing file at the target path is overwritten; if FALSE, the function errors out.


format_excel
Logical. If TRUE (default), the function will use more user-friendly format for the spreadsheet.


sheet_name
Character. Name of the worksheet. Default “described_specimens”.


base_font_size
Numeric. Base font size. Default 10.


base_font_name
Character. Base font name. Default “Calibri Light”.


verbose
Logical. Print progress messages. Default TRUE.


filename
Output file base name (with or without “.xlsx”). If NULL, uses “taxon_template” or “_template” when a group is given.


dir
Output directory. If NULL, a directory named after filename (without extension) is created in the working directory. A date-stamped subfolder is created inside.





Value
Invisibly returns the absolute path to the written .xlsx file.


Examples
# Using a data frame
species_df <- data.frame(
  Genus   = c("Ouratea", "Ouratea", "Ouratea"),
  Species = c("acicularis", "acuminata", "cassinefolia"),
  Author  = c("R.G.Chacon & K.Yamam.", "(DC.) Engl.", "(DC.) Engl.")
)

barroso_chars_template(
  species_df = species_df,
  filename   = "Ouratea_template"
)

# Using an Excel file path
barroso_chars_template(
  species_df = "my_species_list.xlsx",
  sheet = 1,
  plant_group = "Ochnaceae",
  filename = "Ouratea_Ochnaceae_template"
)

title: std_dates
text:
barRoso::std_dates()


Description
Cleans the day, month and year columns of herbarium records into whole numbers, fixing the most common errors of these columns, and flags the dates that could not be fixed.


Details
The following changes are made:

Numbers written with zeros or decimals become whole numbers, e.g. "06" and "6.0" into 6, and zeros like "0" or "00", used for unknown days and months, become NA.
Months written as names or Roman numerals in English, Portuguese, Spanish or Latin become numbers, e.g. "Jun", "junho", "junio" and "VI" into 6.
Days and months in the wrong columns are swapped, which can only be known when the month is greater than 12 and the day is not, e.g. month 23 and day 7 into day 23 and month 7.
Missing days, months and years are taken from eventDate, e.g. "1995-07-23" or "23/7/1995", when present.
Values that are not possible dates become NA, e.g. month 14 with day 15, day 31 in April, day 29 in February of a year that is not a leap year, or years before 1700 or after the current year.

The column dateIssues tells what was changed in each record, e.g. "day and month swapped", "invalid month", "invalid day", "invalid year" or "date from eventDate", and is NA for records without changes beyond the number format.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame with herbarium records.


colname_day
Column name for the day of collection (default: "day").


colname_month
Column name for the month of collection (default: "month").


colname_year
Column name for the year of collection (default: "year").


colname_eventDate
Column name for the date of collection, used to fill in missing days, months and years. Ignored when not in df (default: "eventDate").


rm_original_column
Logical; if FALSE, the original columns are kept with the suffix Original, e.g. monthOriginal (default: TRUE).





Value
The data frame with the day, month and year as whole numbers, and the column dateIssues after them.


Examples
df <- data.frame(day = c("07", "23", "00", "31", NA),
                 month = c("06", "7", "Jun", "IV", NA),
                 year = c("1995", "2001", "1987.0", "2010", NA),
                 eventDate = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, "1995-07-23"))
std_dates(df)

title: std_coordinates
text:
barRoso::std_coordinates()


Description
Checks the geographic coordinates of biodiversity records following the workflow of the bdc package. Coordinates with latitude and longitude transposed or with inverted signs are fixed, while all other problems are flagged, so the user knows what was fixed and which records need attention.


Details
The function applies, in this order:

Parsing of coordinates stored as text, e.g. with decimal commas ("-12,5"). Values that cannot be read as numbers (e.g. "Bloqueada" in speciesLink) are set to NA and flagged.
bdc::bdc_coordinates_empty() and bdc::bdc_coordinates_outOfRange().
bdc::bdc_country_standardized(), used internally to get the country codes (the original country column is not changed).
bdc::bdc_coordinates_transposed(), which FIXES coordinates with latitude and longitude swapped and/or with inverted signs, based on the country of each record.
bdc::bdc_coordinates_country_inconsistent(), for coordinates falling outside the country informed in the record.
bdc::bdc_coordinates_precision(), for coordinates with few decimals.
CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(), with the tests used in the space module of bdc that do not need downloads: country capitals, country and province centroids, biodiversity institutions, zero and equal coordinates, and the GBIF headquarters.

The flag columns follow the bdc convention, where TRUE means the record passed the test and FALSE means it was flagged: .coordinates_empty, .coordinates_outOfRange, .coordinates_country_inconsistent, .rou, .equ, .zer, .cap, .cen, .gbf, .inst. As in bdc, the column coordinates_transposed has no leading dot because the problem was fixed (FALSE means the coordinates were corrected). So, the output can be used directly with bdc::bdc_summary_col() and bdc::bdc_filter_out_flags().
A column coordinateIssues describes in words what was fixed or flagged in each record, e.g. "transposed, fixed (latitude and longitude swapped); low precision".


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame containing biodiversity records.


colname_decimalLatitude
Column name for latitude in decimal degrees (default: "decimalLatitude").


colname_decimalLongitude
Column name for longitude in decimal degrees (default: "decimalLongitude").


colname_country
Column name for country (default: "country"). If the column is not found, the country-based tests are skipped.


colname_scientificName
Column name for the taxon name, used to report the transposed coordinates (default: "scientificName").


fix_transposed
Logical; if TRUE, fix transposed coordinates (default: TRUE).


check_country
Logical; if TRUE, flag coordinates outside the informed country (default: TRUE).


check_space
Logical; if TRUE, flag coordinates at capitals, centroids, institutions, zero or equal coordinates and GBIF headquarters (default: TRUE).


min_decimals
Minimum number of decimals of both latitude and longitude, below which coordinates are flagged as low precision (default: 2).


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, the original coordinate columns are removed. If FALSE, they are retained with the *Original suffix (default: FALSE).





Value
The input data frame with numeric coordinates, with transposed coordinates fixed, plus the bdc-like flag columns and the column coordinateIssues.


Examples
df <- read.csv("gbif_download.csv")
df_coords <- std_coordinates(df)

# Summarize the flags and remove flagged records with bdc
df_coords <- bdc::bdc_summary_col(df_coords)
df_clean <- bdc::bdc_filter_out_flags(df_coords, col_to_remove = "all")

title: std_taxa
text:
barRoso::std_taxa()


Description
Cleans and standardizes taxonomic fields in a biodiversity collection dataset. Specifically targets and harmonizes the family, genus, and specificEpithet columns, correcting legacy naming (e.g. Leguminosae → Fabaceae), removing ambiguous entries, and formatting genus/species names for consistency.


Details
This function is part of the barRoso package and is designed to improve the quality of taxon names for reconciliation, querying, and label generation. It removes common taxonomic noise such as uncertain identifiers (e.g. “cf.”, “aff.”, “indet.”), numeric placeholders, and genus-only labels mistakenly stored in the species field. Genus names are capitalized, and legacy family names (like Leguminosae) are standardized to their accepted equivalents (e.g. Fabaceae).


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame with biodiversity collection records.


colname_family
Name of the column containing plant family names (default: "family").


colname_genus
Name of the column containing genus names (default: "genus").


colname_specificEpithet
Name of the column containing specific epithet of the species names (default: "specificEpithet").


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, original columns are removed after cleaning (default: TRUE).





Value
A data frame with cleaned and standardized family, genus, and specificEpithet columns. If rm_original_column = FALSE, original values are retained with a *Original suffix.


Examples
df <- read.csv("taxa.csv")
df_clean <- std_taxa(df,
                     colname_family = "familia",
                     colname_genus = "genero",
                     colname_specificEpithet = "especie",
                     rm_original_column = FALSE)

title: std_collection
text:
barRoso::std_collection()


Description
Cleans and standardizes herbarium acronyms in biodiversity datasets by harmonizing values from the collectionCode and institutionCode fields. The function corrects common issues in GBIF and other aggregated records, replacing ambiguous or placeholder codes with the herbarium acronyms of Index Herbariorum.


Details
This function is part of the barRoso package. Instead of a dictionary of every code, it uses regular expressions that generalize across datasets, in the following order:

Aggregated collections like "Tropicos" or "MO-Duplicates" are replaced with the herbarium of the specimen given in institutionCode (e.g. "NY"), or with "MO" when it is missing.
Generic words like "Botany", "Herbarium", "Vascular Plants" or "PNGplants" are replaced with the acronym in institutionCode or, when missing, with the acronym at the beginning of catalogNumber (e.g. "U.1317533" into "U") or in occurrenceID (e.g. "urn:catalog:INB:...").
Names of collections, like "F-Seedplants", "BHCB-Fanerogamas", "INPA-Carpoteca", "R-Tipos", "UIS-H" or "BSMvplantscoll", are reduced to the herbarium acronym. Codes of wood collections, like "INPAw", are kept.
Names of herbaria and institutions, like "Herbario INPA", "Herbario Nacional de Costa Rica (CR)" or "Instituto de Botanica de Sao Paulo", are replaced with the acronym given in the name or with the known acronym.
Codes that are not acronyms, like observation projects ("Observations", "Dados de Pesquisa SISBio"), companies ("Ecopetrol S.A") or numbers, are replaced with the acronym in institutionCode or catalogNumber, or with NA.

The columns catalogNumber and occurrenceID are used when present.
Catalog numbers in catalogNumber are then written without spaces and punctuation, with the standardized acronym of the herbarium when they are just numbers, e.g. "181351" into "HUA181351", "HATM 003653" into "HATM003653", "ANDES-H:6594" into "ANDESH6594", "L.2049875" into "L2049875", "CANB 490096.1" into "CANB4900961" and "barcode-00064442" into "A00064442". Collector names with numbers, e.g. "M. A. Chocce 536", are not catalog numbers and become NA. The original catalog numbers are kept in catalogNumberOriginal along with collectionCodeOriginal.
By default (index_herbariorum = TRUE), the results of these steps are checked against all herbaria of the Index Herbariorum API, downloaded at once and kept during the R session, which needs internet access:

Codes in collectionCode found in Index Herbariorum get its spelling (e.g. "UnB" into "UNB"). The code of Index Herbariorum identifies the herbarium, so it goes into collectionCode, and institutionCode is not changed by this check.
Codes not found are looked for by the full name of the institution in the original collectionCode or institutionCode, when the name belongs to a single herbarium, as universities may have several (e.g. "Universidade de Sao Paulo").
The column institutionName gets the name of the institution in Index Herbariorum, and the new column indexHerbariorum is FALSE for codes not found, which are left as they were, for checking.
The original collectionCode is always kept in collectionCodeOriginal, whatever the value of rm_original_column.

If the API cannot be reached, a warning is given and the codes are not checked.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame with biodiversity specimen records.


colname_collectionCode
Name of the column containing collection codes (default: "collectionCode").


colname_institutionCode
Name of the column containing institution codes (default: "institutionCode").


index_herbariorum
Logical; if TRUE, checks the codes against the API of Index Herbariorum (see Details) (default: TRUE). Use FALSE to work offline with just the regular expressions.


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, original columns are removed after cleaning (default: TRUE). The original collectionCode is always kept with index_herbariorum = TRUE, the default.





Value
A data frame with standardized collection codes in the collectionCode column. If rm_original_column = FALSE, the original values are saved with a *Original suffix. With index_herbariorum = TRUE, it also has the columns collectionCodeOriginal, institutionName and indexHerbariorum.


Examples
df <- data.frame(collectionCode = c("Tropicos", "Botany", "F-Seedplants",
                                    "Herbario INPA", "Observations"),
                 institutionCode = c("NY", NA, "F", "INPA", "iNaturalist"),
                 catalogNumber = c("100595392", "U.1317533", "V0059731F",
                                   "123", "340214363"))
std_collection(df, index_herbariorum = FALSE)$collectionCode


# Checking the codes against Index Herbariorum (the default)
std_collection(df)

title: dms_to_decimal
text:
barRoso::dms_to_decimal()


Description
Converts geographic coordinates written in degrees, minutes and seconds (e.g. "22º22´55´´S", "53°45'W", "12 30 15.5 S") into decimal degrees (e.g. -22.381944), as they are often recorded in herbarium labels and in the verbatim coordinates of databases like REFLORA, JABOT and speciesLink.


Details
The function recognizes:

degree symbols º, °, ˚ or d; minute symbols ’, ´, ′, ’ or m; second symbols “, '', ´´, ″, ” or s, or just spaces between the numbers;
decimal minutes or seconds, with dot or comma (e.g. "12°30,5'S");
the hemisphere as N, S, E, W, or O (oeste) and L (leste) as in Portuguese and Spanish, before or after the numbers, or a minus sign;
coordinates already in decimal degrees (e.g. "-12.5"), which are kept.

Values that cannot be converted, or with minutes or seconds of 60 or more, or out of the range of latitude (±90) or longitude (±180), are returned as NA, with a warning.
When the hemisphere is not written (e.g. "22º22´55´´"), the result is positive, unless it is given in hemisphere, e.g. hemisphere = "S" for latitudes of Brazilian specimens.


Arguments







Argument
Description




x
Character vector of coordinates.


type
Either "latitude", "longitude" or "auto" (default). It is used to check the range of the coordinates; with "auto", the range depends on the hemisphere (±90 for N and S, ±180 otherwise).


hemisphere
Optional hemisphere ("N", "S", "E" or "W") for the coordinates written without hemisphere or sign.


digits
Number of decimal places of the result (default: 6, about 10 cm).





Value
A numeric vector of coordinates in decimal degrees.


Examples
dms_to_decimal(c("22º22´55´´S", "53°45'W", "12 30 15.5 S", "S 8°30.5'", "-55.602222"))

# Latitudes without hemisphere
dms_to_decimal(c("22º22´55´´", "1º42´12´´"), type = "latitude", hemisphere = "S")

# Longitude in Portuguese (O = oeste = west)
dms_to_decimal("43º40'49''O")

title: std_identifiedBy
text:
barRoso::std_identifiedBy()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the identifiedBy field in biodiversity collection data, using the same name-cleaning rules of std_recordedBy(). Each determiner name is formatted with abbreviated initials before the surname (e.g. "Cardoso, D.B.O.S." into "D. B. O. S. Cardoso").


Details
Unlike std_recordedBy(), no additional column is created when there are several determiners. All names are kept in the same cell, each one standardized and joined as "D. Cardoso & L. P. Queiroz" or "A. Pott, V. J. Pott & D. Cardoso".
Before standardizing the names, the function removes information that often comes along with the determiner in the identifiedBy field, such as the prefix "det.", herbarium acronyms in parentheses (e.g. "(MO)"), and determination dates (e.g. "/VI-2011", ", 2006", "18 Jun 1996"). Missing or anonymous determiners are returned as NA.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame containing biodiversity records.


colname_identifiedBy
Column name for the determiner (default: "identifiedBy").


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, the original column is removed after cleaning. If FALSE, it is retained with the *Original suffix (default: FALSE).





Value
A data frame with the standardized determiner names.


Examples
df <- read.csv("herbarium_records.csv")
df_clean <- std_identifiedBy(df,
                             colname_identifiedBy = "identifiedBy",
                             rm_original_column = FALSE)

title: barroso_write_specimens
text:
barRoso::barroso_write_specimens()


Description
Writes the lists of examined specimens of one, several or all species of a database of herbarium records in Darwin Core format, as standardized by barroso_std(), into a Word (.docx) file, in the format of a botanical journal, e.g. Systematic Botany, Taxon, Kew Bulletin or Phytotaxa.


Details
The records are formatted with barroso_dwc(), so the columns may also come from other sources, e.g. speciesLink. The columns used are species, country, stateProvince, municipality, locality, decimalLatitude, decimalLongitude, minimumElevationInMeters, maximumElevationInMeters, day, month, year, reproductiveCondition, recordedBy, addCollector, recordNumber, collectionCode and catalogNumber; and, when present, the columns of barroso_flag_duplicates() with all herbaria of each specimen (duplicateCollectionCodes, duplicateCatalogNumbers). The author of each species comes from scientificNameAuthorship, acceptedScientificName or scientificName.
Duplicates of the same collection (same collector and number, or same collector, date and locality when there is no number) are written once, with all their herbaria. The specimens are ordered by country, state, municipality and date.
Examples of the format of each journal:
Systematic Botany: Representative Specimens Examined—Brazil. —Bahia: Abaíra, Catolés, 13°23′S, 41°48′W, 1200 m, 8 May 1994 (fl), D.B.O.S. Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). (header and states in small capitals, countries in bold, collectors and numbers in italics, as also in Taxon and Acta Botanica Brasilica) Taxon: Additional specimens examined. – BRAZIL. BAHIA: Abaíra, Catolés, 13°23′S, 41°48′W, 1200 m a.s.l., 8 May 1994 (fl.), D.B.O.S. Cardoso & al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Kew Bulletin: SPECIMENS EXAMINED. BRAZIL. Bahia: Abaíra, Catolés, 13°23’S, 41°48’W, 1200 m, 8 May 1994 (fl.), D. B. O. S. Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Phytotaxa: Additional specimens examined:―BRAZIL. Bahia: Abaíra: Catolés, …, 8 May 1994 (fl), D.B.O.S. Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Brittonia: Additional specimens examined.—BRAZIL. Bahia: …, 8 May 1994 [fl], D. B. O. S. Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Candollea: Additional specimens examined. – Brazil. Bahia: …, 13°23’S 41°48’W, 1200 m, 8.V.1994, fl., Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Edinburgh Journal of Botany: Additional specimens examined. BRAZIL. Bahia: …, 8 v 1994 (fl), Cardoso et al. 2066 (HUEFS, RB). Systematics and Biodiversity: Additional specimens examined. BRAZIL. Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame of herbarium records in Darwin Core format, e.g. the output of barroso_std() or barroso_dwc(). Not needed when path is given.


path
Path to an .xlsx, .xls or .csv file with the herbarium records, used when df is NULL.


sheet
Sheet name or index of the .xlsx file. Default 1.


species
Character vector of species names, with or without authors (e.g. "Ormosia arborea"), to write the specimens of just these species. If NULL (default), the specimens of all species are written.


journal
Name of the journal whose format is followed, as in recent papers of the journal: "Systematic Botany" (default), "Acta Botanica Brasilica", "Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden", "Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society", "Brazilian Journal of Botany", "Brittonia", "Candollea", "Edinburgh Journal of Botany", "Kew Bulletin", "Nordic Journal of Botany", "Phytotaxa", "PhytoKeys", "Plant Ecology and Evolution", "Rodriguesia", "Systematics and Biodiversity", "Taxon" or "Willdenowia". The name can be written in any case, with or without accents, and abbreviated (e.g. "systematic botany", "Kew", "Edinburgh", "Rodriguésia").


header
Text of the header before the specimens, e.g. "Additional specimens examined", "Paratypes" or "Selected specimens", written with the format and punctuation of the journal. If NULL (default), the header of the journal, e.g. "Representative Specimens Examined" in Systematic Botany. Use "" to write no header.


language
Language of the section header, months and countries: "en" (default) or "pt".


catalog_numbers
Logical. If TRUE (default), the catalog numbers are written after each herbarium, all of them when the herbarium has several sheets, with the herbaria separated by semicolons, e.g. "(NY barcode 5464648; MO barcodes 45556667, 000894546)" in Systematic Botany or "(IAC no. 14754; NY nos. 1162464, 1162465)" in Brittonia. If FALSE, just the herbaria are written, e.g. "(MO, NY)", with the catalog number of the first herbarium for collections without number.


one_per_municipality
Logical. If TRUE, just one specimen of each municipality is written for each species, the one with the most complete information: state, locality, coordinates, elevation, date (year, month and day), phenology, collector and collector number, and then the most herbaria. Specimens without municipality are not written, so species known only from such specimens are left out. Default FALSE.


dir
Folder where the .docx file is saved. By default, the folder of path, or "results_specimens" when the records are given in df.


filename
Name of the .docx file. By default, the name of path (or "specimens") followed by the journal, e.g. "Ormosia_herbarium_records_Systematic_Botany.docx".


font_family
Font of the document. Default "Times New Roman".


font_size
Font size in points. Default 12.


verbose
Logical. Print progress messages. Default TRUE.





Value
Invisibly, a data frame with the species (species_name) and their examined specimens (specimens_text, one specimen per line). The .docx file is written as a side effect.


Examples
# All species of a database standardized by barRoso
barroso_write_specimens(path = "results/Ormosia_herbarium_records.xlsx",
                        journal = "Systematic Botany")

# Two species, in the format of Kew Bulletin
barroso_write_specimens(df = data_all_clean,
                        species = c("Ormosia arborea", "Ormosia fastigiata"),
                        journal = "Kew Bulletin",
                        dir = "results")

title: barroso_cat
text:
barRoso::barroso_cat()


Description
Merges herbarium records from two or more biodiversity data sources into a single harmonized data frame, keeping the records of each herbarium from a single source, chosen by an order of priority of the sources.


Details
This function aligns column structures, removes redundant records from overlapping herbaria, and merges all sources into a single output. The same herbarium is often in several sources, e.g. the RB collection in JABOT, REFLORA and GBIF, so its records would be repeated. Overlapping herbaria are found by their collectionCode and kept from a single source, following the order of priority in keep_source, e.g. with keep_source = c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "GBIF"):

the herbaria of JABOT are removed from speciesLink, REFLORA and GBIF;
the remaining herbaria of speciesLink are removed from REFLORA and GBIF;
the remaining herbaria of REFLORA are removed from GBIF.

So each herbarium comes from the first source that has it, and GBIF adds only the herbaria that are in none of the other sources.
Each source is first formatted into Darwin Core column names and values with barroso_dwc(), e.g. the columns of speciesLink downloads (collector, collectornumber, recordedby) are renamed into recordedBy and recordNumber, and the dates and type status of REFLORA and JABOT records are standardized. The sources are recognized by their content, so their names in list_sources can be any name.
Before comparing the sources, the herbarium acronyms in collectionCode of each source are standardized with std_collection(), by default checking them against Index Herbariorum (index_herbariorum = TRUE), so the same herbarium is recognized in all sources, e.g. "MOBOT_BR" in speciesLink and "MO" in GBIF, or "Herbario INPA" and "INPA". The original codes are kept in collectionCodeOriginal, so unvouchered collections like "INPA-Carpoteca" can still be removed by barroso_std().
The identifiers of the records in their sources, occurrenceID in GBIF, REFLORA and JABOT (and gbifID in GBIF), are kept as they are, with the source of each record in datasource, so that the records already in a database can be found when it is updated with new downloads (see the argument database of barroso_std()). Records without a unique identifier, from any source (e.g. speciesLink downloads made with plantR, or some GBIF records without gbifID), are compared with the database by their catalog numbers instead, and a message tells how many there are.
Columns with different types across sources (e.g. numeric year in one source and character in another) are combined as character. A column datasource records the source of each record.


Arguments







Argument
Description




list_sources
A named list of data frames. Each element represents a herbarium data source. The names of the list are used to track the source origin for internal filtering.


keep_source
Character vector with the names of all sources of list_sources, in order of priority, e.g. c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "GBIF"). The herbaria of each source are removed from the sources after it, so each herbarium is kept from the first source that has it.


index_herbariorum
Logical; if TRUE, the herbarium acronyms of each source are checked against the API of Index Herbariorum after the regular expressions of std_collection() (default: TRUE). Use FALSE to work offline.





Value
A harmonized data frame combining all provided herbarium sources, with columns aligned, a datasource column, and optionally filtered to resolve duplicate collections.


Examples
reflora <- refloraR::reflora_records(herbarium = "RB", taxon = "Ormosia", save = FALSE)
jabot <- jabotR::jabot_records(herbarium = "MBM", taxon = "Ormosia", save = FALSE)

combined_df <- barroso_cat(list_sources = list(GBIF = gbif_data,
                                               speciesLink = splink_data,
                                               REFLORA = reflora,
                                               JABOT = jabot),
                           keep_source = c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "GBIF"))

title: Overview
text:
What is barRoso?
barRoso is an R package designed to clean, standardize, and reconcile plant specimen records, especially those retrieved from herbarium databases and biodiversity repositories. Originally developed for GBIF, it is compatible with data from JABOT, SEINet, REFLORA, speciesLink, and others.
The package is named after Brazilian botanist Graziela Maciel Barroso, and also serves as an acronym: Biodiversity Analysis and Record Reconciliation for Organizing Specimen Observations.

title: Overview
text:
What does barRoso do?
barRoso helps users:

Standardize collector and determiner names and collection numbers using regex-based parsing
Harmonize taxonomic, geographic, and temporal fields
Combine records from GBIF, speciesLink and other sources
Flag and remove potential duplicates across herbarium records, highlighting conflicting identifications
Fix and flag geographic coordinates, following the workflow of the bdc package
Generate herbarium labels from fieldbook data
Write lists of examined specimens in the format of 24 botanical journals
Integrate with external taxonomic databases (e.g., LCVP, WFO)
Prepare large-scale biodiversity datasets for publication and analysis

title: Overview
text:
Who should use barRoso?

Taxonomists and herbarium curators
Biodiversity data scientists
Floristic inventory teams
Graduate students and researchers managing field collections

title: Overview
text:
What makes barRoso different?
Unlike other packages that rely on static collector name dictionaries, barRoso uses robust, extensible regular expressions to detect name patterns and correct inconsistencies across data sources. It also includes modular, tidyverse-compatible functions for a reproducible and efficient workflow.

title: Overview
text:
Data Preservation Philosophy
While many data tools prioritize aggressive cleaning, often at the cost of discarding valuable records, barRoso takes a different approach. Its philosophy centers on standardization rather than removal. All herbarium specimens carry potential scientific value, even when incomplete or inconsistently entered. Instead of omitting such records, barRoso focuses on harmonizing fields to enhance comparability across collections. By standardizing collector names, geographic fields, and taxonomic labels, barRoso allows users to flag rather than erase inconsistencies, enabling more transparent workflows and tracing potential misidentifications, especially across distributed duplicates. This inclusive approach honors the archival role of herbaria while facilitating reproducible biodiversity research.

title: About barRoso
text:
Overview
barRoso (Biodiversity Analysis and Record Reconciliation for Organizing Specimen Observations) is an R package that streamlines biodiversity data cleaning, integration, and reconciliation, particularly for herbarium records. The toolkit supports workflows from data curation to label production, helping botanists, curators, and researchers analyze plant specimen collections more efficiently.
Named in honor of Graziela Maciel Barroso, one of Brazil’s most respected botanists, the name barRoso also nods to its native programming environment—R.
The package was originally developed for the JABOT Virtual Herbarium, maintained by the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden, but it is generalizable to other biodiversity repositories such as GBIF, SEINet, REFLORA, and speciesLink. The package was originally developed to support the cleaning and reconciliation of plant specimen records retrieved from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), but its flexible design makes it broadly applicable to other biodiversity data sources. These include national and institutional repositories such as the JABOT Virtual Herbarium, maintained by the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden and REFLORA, as well as SEINet and speciesLink.

text: This article walks through a practical case study using the barRoso package to clean and harmonize plant specimen records downloaded from the REFLORA Virtual Herbarium using the refloraR package.

text:

title: REFLORA Cleaning Workflow
text:

# install.packages("devtools")

library(refloraR)

records <- reflora_records(taxon = "Fabaceae", 
                           herbarium = "RB",
                           save = FALSE)

text:

library(barRoso)

cleaned <- barroso_std(records,
                       colname_recordedBy = "recordedBy",
                       colname_recordNumber = "recordNumber",

                       colname_stateProvince = "stateProvince",
                       flag_duplicates = TRUE,
                       rm_duplicates = FALSE)

table(cleaned$duplicate)
head(cleaned[, c("recordedBy", "recordNumber", "duplicate")])

write.csv(cleaned, "reflora_cleaned.csv", row.names = FALSE)

text:

title: Cleaning GBIF Data
text:
Step 1: Download GBIF Records
Use the rgbif package to download occurrence records. Here’s an example for the Fabaceae family:
# install.packages("rgbif")
library(rgbif)

occ <- occ_search(scientificName = "Fabaceae", limit = 1000, hasCoordinate = TRUE)

table(cleaned$duplicate)

subset(cleaned, identificationConflict %in% TRUE,
       select = c(recordedBy, recordNumber, duplicateIdentifications, duplicateCatalogNumbers))

cleaned <- std_coordinates(cleaned)
table(unlist(strsplit(cleaned$coordinateIssues, "; ")))

title: Generate Herbarium Labels
text:
Overview
The barroso_labels() function generates printable herbarium labels directly from field book spreadsheets or CSV files. Labels include specimen information, taxonomic authority, formatted locality descriptions, and location maps (with greater resolution for USA-based collections).

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
Overview
Taxonomic revisions and descriptions of new species cite the specimens examined for each species, in a format that differs from journal to journal: the header, the case and format (bold, italics, small capitals) of countries, states and collectors, how dates and coordinates are written, and how herbaria are listed.
The function barroso_write_specimens() writes these lists for one, several or all species of a database of herbarium records into a Word (.docx) file, in the format of a chosen journal. This article goes through the whole workflow with two R scripts, using the herbarium records of Luetzelburgia (Leguminosae), a genus of 15 species of South American trees:

01_get_standardized_records_script.R downloads the records from GBIF, REFLORA and JABOT, combines and standardizes them, and saves a spreadsheet;
02_write_examined_specimens_script.R writes the lists of examined specimens from this spreadsheet, in the format of several journals.

Both scripts are run from an RStudio project, e.g. build_herbarium_records_database, with the scripts in a folder scripts and the results saved in a folder results.

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
Script 1: get standardized records
The records are downloaded with plantR (GBIF), refloraR (REFLORA Virtual Herbarium) and jabotR (JABOT, Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden). The list of accepted species comes from Kew’s WCVP, with the package rWCVPdata.
# 01_get_standardized_records_script.R

library(barRoso)
library(refloraR)
library(jabotR)
library(plantR)
library(dplyr)
library(openxlsx)
library(rWCVPdata)

# Create a folder for the results of today
dir <- "results"
folder_name <- paste0(dir, "/", format(Sys.time(), "%d%b%Y"))
if (!dir.exists(folder_name)) dir.create(folder_name, recursive = TRUE)

# All accepted species of Luetzelburgia in WCVP
wcvp_names <- rWCVPdata::wcvp_names
luetz_wcvp <- subset(wcvp_names,
                     genus == "Luetzelburgia" &
                       taxon_rank == "Species" &
                       taxon_status == "Accepted")
luetz_list <- sort(luetz_wcvp$taxon_name)

# GBIF: one search for each species, skipping species without records
data_gbif <- lapply(luetz_list, function(x) {
  gbif <- tryCatch(plantR::rgbif2(species = x, n.records = 5000, force = TRUE,
                                  remove_na = FALSE, save = FALSE, compress = FALSE),
                   error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.data.frame(gbif) || nrow(gbif) == 0) return(NULL)
  gbif
})
names(data_gbif) <- luetz_list
data_gbif <- dplyr::bind_rows(data_gbif, .id = "original_search")

# REFLORA Virtual Herbarium
data_reflora <- refloraR::reflora_records(repatriated = TRUE, taxon = "Luetzelburgia",
                                          indets = TRUE, updates = TRUE,
                                          verbose = TRUE, save = FALSE)
unlink("reflora_download/", recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)

# JABOT
data_jabot <- jabotR::jabot_records(taxon = "Luetzelburgia", indets = TRUE,
                                    updates = TRUE, verbose = TRUE, save = FALSE)
unlink("jabot_download/", recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)

# Combine the sources, keeping GBIF for the herbaria present in more than one
records_list <- list(GBIF = data_gbif,
                     REFLORA = data_reflora,
                     JABOT = data_jabot)
data_all <- barRoso::barroso_cat(list_sources = records_list,
                                 keep_source = c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "GBIF"))

# Standardize collectors, herbaria, places and taxa, and remove duplicates
data_all_clean <- barRoso::barroso_std(data_all,
                                       unvouchered = TRUE,
                                       delunkcoll = TRUE,
                                       flag_duplicates = TRUE,
                                       rm_duplicates = TRUE)

# Fix and flag coordinates
data_all_clean <- barRoso::std_coordinates(data_all_clean)

# Save the database
openxlsx::write.xlsx(data_all_clean,
                     paste0(folder_name, "/Luetzelburgia_herbarium_records.xlsx"))
In November 2026, this script found 3,215 records in GBIF, 1,093 in REFLORA and 351 in JABOT:
#> barroso_cat: removing 1089 records of 39 herbaria from REFLORA also present in GBIF
#> barroso_cat: removing 337 records of 10 herbaria from JABOT also present in GBIF
After the standardization, without duplicates, unvouchered records and records of unknown collectors, the database has 1,202 records of 15 species, from Brazil (1,155), Bolivia (35), Colombia (3) and Guyana (3).

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
Script 2: write the examined specimens
The second script reads the spreadsheet saved by the first one, and writes one .docx file for each journal, in the same folder:
# 02_write_examined_specimens_script.R

library(barRoso)
library(openxlsx)

# The most recent spreadsheet within the results folder
dir <- "results"
records_files <- list.files(dir,
                            pattern = "^Luetzelburgia_herbarium_records[.]xlsx$",
                            recursive = TRUE,
                            full.names = TRUE)
records_file <- records_files[which.max(file.mtime(records_files))]
folder_name <- dirname(records_file)

# Read the records once, so the spreadsheet is not read again for each journal
data_records <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(records_file)

# One Word (.docx) file for each journal. To write just some species, use the
# argument species, e.g. species = c("Luetzelburgia andina", "Luetzelburgia harleyi")
journals <- c("Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden",
              "Systematic Botany",
              "Kew Bulletin",
              "Rodriguesia")

for (journal in journals) {
  barRoso::barroso_write_specimens(
    df = data_records,
    species = NULL,
    journal = journal,
    dir = folder_name,
    filename = paste0("Luetzelburgia_examined_specimens_", gsub("\\s+", "_", journal))
  )
}

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
How the specimens are written

Columns. The function uses the Darwin Core columns species, country, stateProvince, municipality (or county, where GBIF keeps the municipalities of Brazil), locality, decimalLatitude, decimalLongitude, minimumElevationInMeters, maximumElevationInMeters, day, month, year, phenology (or reproductiveCondition), recordedBy, addCollector, recordNumber, collectionCode, catalogNumber. Missing columns are just skipped.
Collectors. The names standardized by barroso_std() (e.g. D. B. O. S. Cardoso) are written as each journal cites them. The additional collectors (addCollector) are written as the name of the second collector, e.g. R.M. Harley & A.M. Giulietti, or as et al. (& al. in Taxon) when there are several, e.g. A. Alves, K. Paixão & E. Consuelo.
Phenology. The phenology in the column phenology (as in records from REFLORA and JABOT) or reproductiveCondition, e.g. fl, fl, fr, flower, fruit or st, is written as in each journal:







Format
Journals




(fl, fr)
Systematic Botany, Phytotaxa, Edinburgh Journal of Botany, Acta Botanica Mexicana, Darwiniana ((veg, fl)), and journals whose papers show no phenology (Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society, Feddes Repertorium, PhytoKeys, Plant Ecology and Evolution, Systematics and Biodiversity, Willdenowia)


(fl., fr.)
Taxon, Kew Bulletin, Acta Botanica Brasilica (after a comma), Botany Letters, Hoehnea, Plant Systematics and Evolution


(fl./fr.)
Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden


(fl. fr.)
Nordic Journal of Botany


(fl and fr)
Brazilian Journal of Botany


[fl, fr]
Brittonia


fl. and fr.
Rodriguésia, and fl., fr. in Candollea, without brackets


Fl., fr.
Acta Amazonica, before the date



In Portuguese and Spanish, and becomes e or y, and sterile (st) becomes est.
Repeated places. Some journals do not repeat the place of the previous specimen: l.c. for the same municipality in Hoehnea, and loc. cit. or ídem for the same locality in Acta Botanica Mexicana and Darwiniana.
Duplicates. Duplicates of the same collection (same species, collector surname and number, or same collector, date and locality when there is no number) are written once, with all their herbaria in alphabetical order, including those found by barroso_flag_duplicates() (duplicateCollectionCodes).
Types. The type status is not written, as types are cited apart from the examined specimens.
Catalog numbers. By default, all catalog numbers are written after their herbarium, e.g. (MO 45556667, 000894546; NY 5464648) in Systematic Botany. With catalog_numbers = FALSE, just the herbaria are written, and for collections without number, the catalog number of the first herbarium, e.g. R. Spruce s.n. (K000892474, LD), so that the specimen can be found.
Order. Specimens are ordered by country, state, municipality and date. Records not identified to species are skipped.
Species. For each species, a heading with the species name in italics and its author (from scientificNameAuthorship, acceptedScientificName or scientificName) is followed by the paragraph of its specimens.

The function returns, invisibly, a data frame with the species and their specimens, one per line, which can be checked in R:
res <- barroso_write_specimens(path = "results/01Nov2026/Luetzelburgia_herbarium_records.xlsx",
                               species = "Luetzelburgia andina", verbose = FALSE)
cat(res$specimens_text)

title: Write Lists of Examined Specimens
text:
Tips

Standardize the database first with barroso_std(), so that collectors, herbarium acronyms and places are written consistently, and duplicates are removed.
Check the countries and states of the database before writing: the specimens are cited as they are in the data.
For the paratypes of a new species, use species and header = "Paratypes".
For widespread species with many collections, use one_per_municipality = TRUE to cite a representative specimen of each municipality, e.g. with header = "Representative specimens examined". On the Ormosia dataset, 7,621 specimens of 122 species become 2,055 specimens of 105 species.

title: Write Taxonomic Descriptions
text:
Overview
The barroso_write_descriptions() function is a powerful tool in the barRoso package for generating automated morphological descriptions from structured Excel data. It transforms taxonomic and morphological character data into standardized, publication-ready species descriptions in Word document format.

title: Write Taxonomic Descriptions
text:
Key Features

Automatically generates species descriptions from morphological Excel data
Groups related characters and avoids term repetition
Combines measurements (length × width) with proper units and symbols
Formats measurement ranges with en dashes (e.g., “4.3–14.5 cm”)
Writes rare small and large values between parentheses, as usual in taxonomic descriptions (e.g., “(2–)6–40(–55) m”)
Handles complex hierarchical character structures
Merges duplicate species entries intelligently
Customizable text formatting (bold, italic) for different description elements
Exports professionally formatted Word (.docx) documents

title: Write Taxonomic Descriptions
text:
Usage
library(barRoso)

# Generate descriptions for all species
descriptions <- barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
  character_cols = 4:20
)

# Generate descriptions only for specific species
descriptions <- barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species"),
  character_cols = 3:15,
  species_filter = c("Ouratea concinna", "Ouratea coarctata")
)

# Customize formatting and output
descriptions <- barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = 1:3,
  character_cols = 4:25,
  font_family = "Arial",
  font_size = 11,
  species_bold = TRUE,
  species_italic = TRUE,
  group_bold = FALSE,
  group_italic = TRUE,
  description_bold = FALSE,
  description_italic = FALSE,
  filename = "MySpeciesDescriptions",
  dir = "Output"
)

title: Write Taxonomic Descriptions
text:
Output
Returns a data frame with:

species_name: Full species name with authorship
description_plain: Plain text version of the description

Also creates a Word document (.docx) saved to the specified directory with:

Species names formatted following botanical conventions
Morphological descriptions organized by character groups, with single traits separated by commas and parts with their own traits after semicolons
Measurements and counts pooled into ranges with units, with rare values between parentheses
Hierarchical characters grouped logically

Data Format Requirements

# Simple characters: "HABIT", "LEAF shape"
# Measurements: "LEAF length (cm)", "LEAF width (mm)"
# Hierarchical: "LEAF MARGINS", "FLOWER SEPALS shape"
# Complex hierarchy: "FLOWER SEPALS BASE shape", "FLOWER SEPALS APEX shape"

Measurements
Each row of the spreadsheet is one specimen, and each cell of a measurement column has the measurements of that specimen.

Several measurements of the same specimen

These are the four specimens of Ouratea hostilis in the example dataset chars_dataset. The values of all specimens of a species are pooled to build its range. Spaces around the | are optional, and a decimal point must be used (4.5, not 4,5).


Rare values between parentheses
Taxonomic descriptions usually give the common range of a measurement, with rare small and large values between parentheses, e.g. Tree (2–)6–40 m tall, leaflets (7.8–)12–39.5 × (3.7–)5–13(–15.5) cm. barroso_write_descriptions() writes them in two ways:

Marked in the spreadsheet: values written as in a description, e.g. (5–)7–38(–45) or (2–)6 | 9 | 12, are always written as rare values when they are beyond the range of the other values of the species. Use this when you know a measurement is unusual, even with few specimens.
Automatic: when a species has at least extremes_min_n values (default 10), the range covers the values from the 10th to the 90th percentile (extremes = c(0.1, 0.9)), and the smallest and largest values outside it are written between parentheses. The limits of the range are always measured values. For example, the 11 values 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 20, 40 and 55 m become (2–)6–40(–55) m. With fewer values, the range goes from the smallest to the largest value (2–55 m).

# Percentiles 5 and 95, from 20 values per species
barroso_write_descriptions(xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
                           species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
                           character_cols = 4:30,
                           extremes = c(0.05, 0.95),
                           extremes_min_n = 20)

# Just the rare values marked in the spreadsheet
barroso_write_descriptions(xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
                           species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
                           character_cols = 4:30,
                           extremes = NULL)


Counts
Counts, like the pairs of secondary veins, the stamens or the flowers of an inflorescence, are also pooled into ranges, with rare values between parentheses, when they are in their own columns with just numbers. Any text goes in another column:

The lowercase words at the end of the column name are written after the range, e.g. secondary venation 6–12 pairs, curved distally towards the marginal vein and 10–25 flowers, except number and count, e.g. stamen 10. A column of text with numbers, like 6 - 12 pairs, curved distally towards the marginal vein, is written as it is, and the phrases of the specimens are listed one after the other.
In the Ouratea dataset of the dry diagonal of Brazil, most species have 1 to 4 specimens, so automatic rare values appear only where at least 10 measurements were taken, e.g. the leaf blades of Ouratea hostilis, with 12 values: (4.3–)4.7–13(–14.5) × 1–4.1 cm.

title: Write Taxonomic Descriptions
text:
Notes

Uses parsing of column names to group related characters
Measurements sharing the same base name are automatically combined (e.g., “LEAF length” and “LEAF width” become “X × Y cm”)
ALL CAPS terms in column names are used for hierarchical grouping
Within each organ, single traits are separated by commas (e.g. Stipule 1 pair, lateral to petiole, 11–16 × 2–3 mm, lanceolate, base truncate, apex acute), while parts with their own traits in lowercase (e.g. HABIT STEM color, LEAF PETIOLE shape) start after a semicolon (e.g. Shrub 1.8 m tall, erect, branched; stem striated, gray, glabrous). A part without traits in lowercase, like STIPULE BASE, is a single trait (base truncate)
Creates date-stamped folders to organize output by processing date
Maintains original column order while intelligently grouping related items

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Overview
Geographic coordinates of herbarium specimens often have errors: latitude and longitude swapped, a missing minus sign, coordinates pointing to the herbarium that houses the specimen or to the center of a country, or just too few decimals. The function std_coordinates() checks the coordinates following the workflow of the bdc package and, in line with the barRoso philosophy, it fixes what can be safely fixed and flags everything else, so you know what was changed and which records need attention.

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Installation of the suggested packages
std_coordinates() uses packages that are not installed with barRoso by default:
install.packages(c("bdc", "CoordinateCleaner", "rnaturalearth", "rnaturalearthdata"))
install.packages("rnaturalearthhires", repos = "https://ropensci.r-universe.dev")

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Usage
library(barRoso)

df <- read.csv("gbif.csv")

df_coords <- std_coordinates(df)

# What was fixed or flagged
table(unlist(strsplit(df_coords$coordinateIssues, "; ")))
Custom column names can be given, e.g. for raw speciesLink downloads:
df_coords <- std_coordinates(splink,
                             colname_decimalLatitude = "latitude",
                             colname_decimalLongitude = "longitude",
                             colname_scientificName = "scientificname")

text:
What is checked
The checks are applied in this order:









Step
Check

Result




1
Coordinates stored as text, e.g. "-12,5" with decimal comma, or "Bloqueada" in speciesLink
—
converted into numbers; values that are not numbers are set to NA and flagged


2
Empty coordinates
bdc::bdc_coordinates_empty()

3
Out of range coordinates (latitude beyond ±90 or longitude beyond ±180)
bdc::bdc_coordinates_outOfRange()

4
Latitude and longitude transposed, or with inverted signs
bdc::bdc_coordinates_transposed()

5
Coordinates outside the country informed in the record
bdc::bdc_coordinates_country_inconsistent()

6
Low precision, i.e. fewer decimals than min_decimals (default: 2)
bdc::bdc_coordinates_precision()

7

CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(), as in the space module of bdc
flagged



Country names are standardized with bdc::bdc_country_standardized() just for these checks; the country column of your data is not changed.

Transposed coordinates
A record is tested when its coordinates fall outside its country (considering a buffer of 0.2 degrees). As in bdc, seven combinations are tried, in this order, and the first one falling inside the country is kept:

sign of latitude inverted
sign of longitude inverted
signs of latitude and longitude inverted
latitude and longitude swapped
latitude and longitude swapped, and sign of latitude inverted
latitude and longitude swapped, and sign of longitude inverted
latitude and longitude swapped, and signs inverted

For example, a record from Brazil at latitude 10.2 and longitude -59.35 falls in the Atlantic Ocean; with the sign of the latitude inverted (-10.2), it falls in Brazil, so it is fixed.






Note



The steps 4 and 5 follow the same logic of the corresponding bdc functions (same Natural Earth map, buffers and combinations), but are run by barRoso itself. In bdc 1.1.6, bdc_coordinates_transposed() writes the fixed coordinates back into the wrong records when several countries are corrected at once, and bdc_coordinates_country_inconsistent() fails or flags correct coordinates with recent versions of dplyr.




Coordinates outside the informed country
Coordinates are flagged when they fall outside the country informed in the record, considering a buffer of 0.1 degrees to avoid flagging records close to the borders or on the coast.

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Using the flags with bdc
Since the flag columns follow the bdc convention, you can summarize and filter them with bdc:
# Column .summary is FALSE when any test failed
df_coords <- bdc::bdc_summary_col(df_coords)

# Keep only records that passed all tests
df_clean <- bdc::bdc_filter_out_flags(df_coords, col_to_remove = "all")
However, in line with the barRoso philosophy, consider reviewing the flagged records before removing them: a record with low precision or at a province centroid may still be useful, e.g. for mapping at the country or state level.

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
section: Coordinates in degrees, minutes and seconds
text:
Coordinates in degrees, minutes and seconds
Herbarium labels and the verbatim coordinates of databases like REFLORA and JABOT are often written in degrees, minutes and seconds. The function dms_to_decimal() converts them into decimal degrees, recognizing the many symbols and hemisphere letters found in herbarium data, also in Portuguese (O for oeste, L for leste):
dms_to_decimal(c("22º22´55´´S", "53°45'W", "12 30 15.5 S", "S 8°30.5'", "43º40'49''O", "-55.602222"))
#> [1] -22.381944 -53.750000 -12.504306  -8.508333 -43.680278 -55.602222
When the hemisphere is not written, as in many REFLORA latitudes (e.g. "22º22´55´´"), it can be given:
dms_to_decimal(reflora$verbatimLatitude, type = "latitude", hemisphere = "S")
Invalid values, like "60º6´61´´W" (61 seconds) or latitudes beyond 90°, become NA with a warning. Checked against 423 REFLORA and JABOT records that have both verbatim and decimal coordinates, all valid values match the decimal coordinates of the databases.
Unlike std_coordinates(), dms_to_decimal() works on a single vector of coordinates, so it can be used before checking the coordinates:
df$decimalLatitude <- dms_to_decimal(df$verbatimLatitude, type = "latitude")
df$decimalLongitude <- dms_to_decimal(df$verbatimLongitude, type = "longitude")
df <- std_coordinates(df)

title: Fix and Flag Coordinates
text:
Arguments

df: A data frame with biodiversity records
colname_decimalLatitude, colname_decimalLongitude: Columns of the coordinates in decimal degrees
colname_country: Column of the country; without it, the country-based checks are skipped
colname_scientificName: Column of the taxon name
fix_transposed: Fix transposed coordinates (default: TRUE)
check_country: Flag coordinates outside the informed country (default: TRUE)
check_space: Flag capitals, centroids, institutions, zero and equal coordinates, and the GBIF headquarters (default: TRUE)
min_decimals: Minimum number of decimals of both coordinates (default: 2)
rm_original_column: Remove the original coordinate columns (default: FALSE)

title: Flag Identifications by Specialists
text:
Overview
Not all identifications of herbarium specimens are equally reliable. A name given by a specialist of the group is much more likely to be right than a name given when the specimen was collected, or copied to the duplicates sent to other herbaria. For distribution maps, niche models, conservation assessments or checklists, you may want to know which records were identified by specialists, or to use just those.
barroso_flag_specialists() flags all records identified by the specialists you give, each one within their taxa of expertise, or keeps just these records:
specialists <- data.frame(
  specialist = c("D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "H. C. Lima"),
  taxon = c("Ormosia", "Swartzia", "Leguminosae"))

df <- barroso_flag_specialists(df, specialists)

# Just the records identified by the specialists
reliable <- barroso_flag_specialists(df, specialists, filter = TRUE)
It works with any data frame, but works best with records standardized with barroso_std(), where the names of collectors and determiners, the additional collectors and the families are already standardized, e.g. Lima, H.C. and H.C. de Lima are both H. C. Lima.

A record identified by a specialist outside their taxa is not flagged, e.g. a Virola identified by a specialist of Ormosia. Names of people are compared by surname and first initial, so D. B. O. S. Cardoso matches D. Cardoso, and families also by their alternative names (Leguminosae and Fabaceae, Compositae and Asteraceae, Gramineae and Poaceae, Palmae and Arecaceae, Cruciferae and Brassicaceae, Guttiferae and Clusiaceae, Labiatae and Lamiaceae, Umbelliferae and Apiaceae).

text:
What is flagged
Three new columns are added after identifiedBy:

specialistIdentification: TRUE for the records identified by the specialists.
specialistName: the specialist, as written in specialists, e.g. H. C. Lima, or several separated by |, e.g. D. B. O. S. Cardoso | H. C. Lima for D. Cardoso & H. C. Lima.
specialistEvidence: how the record was identified by the specialist:








specialistEvidence
Records




identifiedBy
The specialist is in identifiedBy, also among several determiners, e.g. D. Cardoso & L. P. Queiroz


recordedBy
Without determiner, collected by the specialist, as main (recordedBy) or additional collector (addCollector), as specialists usually identify their own collections


duplicate
A duplicate of the same specimen, with the same name, was identified or collected by the specialist, e.g. the duplicate at MO of a specimen identified by the specialist at RB



The duplicates are found with the columns of barroso_flag_duplicates() (duplicateGroup), so run it before. A duplicate with another name is not flagged, as the specialist did not agree with it.

title: Flag Identifications by Specialists
text:
Inside barroso_std()
With flag_specialists = TRUE, barroso_std() flags the identifications of the specialists after flagging the duplicates and before removing them. So a record kept from a block of duplicates is flagged when one of its removed duplicates, with the same name, was identified by a specialist:
data_all <- barroso_std(data_all,
                        rm_duplicates = TRUE,
                        specialists = specialists,
                        flag_specialists = TRUE)

table(data_all$specialistEvidence)
The same specialists are used to resolve conflicting duplicates, as described in Detect and Flag Duplicates.
For example, for 10,294 records of Ormosia from GBIF, speciesLink, REFLORA and JABOT, with D. B. O. S. Cardoso as a specialist of Ormosia and H. C. Lima of Leguminosae:
barroso_flag_specialists: 1072 of 10294 records identified by the specialists (595 as determiners, 226 as collectors without determiner, 251 by a duplicate)
After removing the duplicates, 514 of the 6,769 records kept are flagged: 367 identified by the specialists, 95 collected by them, and 52 whose identification comes from a removed duplicate.

title: Flag Identifications by Specialists
text:
Tips

Give each specialist with all their taxa of expertise, in several rows.
Determiners written with the surname alone, e.g. Stirton, are not matched, as the first initial is needed to tell apart people with the same surname. Check the most frequent determiners of your data with sort(table(df$identifiedBy), decreasing = TRUE).
Records identified by specialists can also be selected after barroso_std() with subset(df, specialistIdentification).

title: Detect and Flag Duplicates
Detect and Flag Duplicates
text:
How duplicates are found







Case
Records are duplicates when they share




With collector number
the collector (recordedBy) and the collector number (recordNumber)


Without collector number
the species name, the collector and the full collection date (year, month and day)




Records with unknown collector (NA or "Unknown") are never treated as duplicates, as "Unknown 1" in two herbaria are most likely different collections.
Without collector number, the full date is required, because the same collector may have collected the same species in different days.
The specific epithet is taken from specificEpithet or, when missing, from a binomial in the column species, as in GBIF downloads, which have no specificEpithet column.


The same collector written in other ways
Even after standardizing, the same collector can be written in other ways in different herbaria, e.g. L. Queiroz and L. P. Queiroz, or A. D. Salinas, A. Delgado Salinas and A. Delgado-Salinas, so their duplicates would not be found. They cannot simply be taken as the same person: L. Queiroz 12456 may be a collection of Luis Queiroz, and L. P. Queiroz 12456 of Luciano Paganucci de Queiroz, with the same number by chance.
So, before finding duplicates, barroso_std() makes a deep search across the whole data (not in chunks) for the same collector written in other ways (match_collectors = TRUE, the default):

Each name is temporarily written in the same form: its initials and last surname. The first surnames of compound surnames become initials, so A. Delgado-Salinas, A. Delgado Salinas and A. D. Salinas are all A D + Salinas, while L. P. Queiroz is L P + Queiroz.
Records with the same first initial, last surname and collector number, but written in other ways, are compared.
A record gets the most complete name only when it has the same date (day, month and year) or the same municipality of a record with that name, which shows that they are the same collection.
When several complete names fit, e.g. E. H. A. Rodrigues and E. M. A. Rodrigues for E. A. Rodrigues, the one that agrees the most with the record is chosen, scored with 4 points for the same full date, 2 for the same year and month, 1 for the same year, and 1 for the same municipality. Only when different people agree as much, the record is kept as it is.

Result

Both L. P. Queiroz, and duplicates

Kept as they are: probably two people

Both A. Delgado-Salinas, the most frequent form in the data


E. A. Rodrigues 341, 15 Sep 1995, Jaboticabal; E. H. A. Rodrigues 341, 15 Sep 1995, Jaboticabal; E. M. A. Rodrigues 341, 25 Sep 1995, Jaboticabal
E. H. A. Rodrigues, with the same date and municipality (5 points), rather than E. M. A. Rodrigues, with the same month and municipality (3 points)


L. Queiroz 1, with the same date and municipality of both L. P. Queiroz 1 and L. M. Queiroz 1
Kept as it is: the collector cannot be known


D. Cardoso 2344 and D. Queiroz Cardoso 2344, same date
Kept as they are: Queiroz is a surname, not an initial



The most complete name has more initials, e.g. L. P. Queiroz rather than L. Queiroz, but a name only gets initials written as such, not surnames turned into initials, as in D. Queiroz Cardoso. For the same initials written in other ways, e.g. B. M. T. Walter and B. M. Teles Walter, the name most frequent in the whole data is kept, with accents when they differ just by them (F. Falcón rather than F. Falcon).
For 10,294 records of Ormosia from GBIF, speciesLink, REFLORA and JABOT, 205 records of 82 names got a more complete name, e.g. R. Fróes into R. L. Fróes (33 records), C. Dick into C. W. Dick and A. A. Santos into A. Amaral-Santos, and 183 more records were found in blocks of duplicates. A message tells how many records got another name, with examples. Use match_collectors = FALSE to skip this step.

Flagging duplicates
df_flagged <- barroso_flag_duplicates(df)

# View flagged rows
subset(df_flagged, duplicate == TRUE)

# View blocks of duplicates with conflicting identifications

# Go directly to the conflicts that need checking: the blocks whose name
# cannot be chosen, as their names are equally frequent

The herbarium acronym is pasted before each catalog number, except when the catalog number already starts with it (e.g. RB00123, K000555). Records that are not duplicates also receive their own herbarium and catalog number in these two columns, so the columns are complete for the whole dataset.

Conflicting identifications
A block has identificationConflict = TRUE when its duplicates are identified as:

different species, e.g. Ormosia arborea and Ormosia nitida; or
different genera, e.g. Ormosia arborea and Swartzia apetala in block 1.

A duplicate identified just to genus does not conflict with a complete name of the same genus. That is why block 2, with Ormosia and Ormosia nitida, has no conflict: the genus-only record is just less complete.
Names are compared exactly, so spelling variants (e.g. Ormosia trifoliata and Ormosia trifoliolata) are also flagged. This helps finding misspelled names, besides misidentifications.


Conflicts that need checking
Not every conflict needs your attention. In block 1, Ormosia arborea is given by three duplicates and Swartzia apetala by one, so the rules below can choose Ormosia arborea. But when the names are equally frequent, e.g. two duplicates as Ormosia arborea and two as Ormosia fastigiata, no rule can tell which name is correct.
barroso_flag_duplicates() marks these blocks with identificationUnresolved = TRUE, in all their records, whether or not duplicates are removed. So you can go directly to them with a single filter:
to_check <- subset(df_flagged, identificationUnresolved %in% TRUE)
to_check[order(to_check$duplicateGroup), ]
The column is FALSE for the other duplicates, including those with conflicts that the rules can resolve, and NA for records that are not duplicates. When you give specialists, their identifications resolve the ties, so only the blocks still unresolved after them are marked. A message also tells how many blocks are unresolved, e.g.:
barroso_flag_duplicates: 14 records in 5 blocks of duplicates, 3 blocks with conflicting identifications, 2 of them unresolved (identificationUnresolved == TRUE)


Fix species names first
Duplicates are compared by their names exactly as written. So two duplicates of the same specimen, one identified with an old name and one with its accepted name, or one with a misspelled name, are taken as a conflict, although both mean the same species:

These false conflicts are a problem when removing duplicates. Two names that are just a synonym and its accepted name are equally frequent, so the block becomes a false tie: it is marked with identificationUnresolved = TRUE, and all its records are kept, or the whole block is removed with rm_tied_conflicts = TRUE, although there is nothing to resolve.
So, run barroso_fix_names() before barroso_std() or barroso_flag_duplicates(). It updates synonyms and misspelled names into accepted names, with the World Checklist of Vascular Plants and the Flora e Funga do Brasil. Then, RB and HUEFS above are both Ormosia fastigiata, MO and K are both Ormosia excelsa, and only real conflicts of identification are left: those that need checking by a taxonomist.
data_all <- barroso_cat(list(REFLORA = data_reflora, JABOT = data_jabot),
                        keep_source = c("JABOT", "REFLORA"))

# 1. Fix synonyms and misspelled names
data_all <- barroso_fix_names(data_all)

# 2. Standardize and remove duplicates, with only real conflicts left
specialists <- data.frame(specialist = c("D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "H. C. Lima"),
                          taxon = c("Ormosia", "Leguminosae"))
data_all <- barroso_std(data_all,
                        rm_duplicates = TRUE,
                        specialists = specialists)

# Real conflicts that need checking
subset(data_all, identificationUnresolved %in% TRUE)
The original names are kept in the column taxonOriginal of barroso_fix_names(), so you still know how each duplicate was identified.

title: Detect and Flag Duplicates
text:
Removing duplicates
With rm_duplicates = TRUE, only one record per block is kept. The record is chosen by the rules below, applied in this order. Each rule only chooses among the records that passed the previous one.
specialists <- data.frame(specialist = c("D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "H. C. Lima"),
                          taxon = c("Ormosia", "Leguminosae"))

df_clean <- barroso_flag_duplicates(df,
                                    rm_duplicates = TRUE,
                                    specialists = specialists,
                                    rm_tied_conflicts = FALSE)

Rule 1: identified to species
Records with a complete species name (genus and specific epithet) are preferred over records identified just to genus.

Block 1: the RB duplicate (Ormosia) is discarded; MO, JBB, K and HUEFS go to rule 2.
Block 2: the ALCB duplicate (Ormosia) is discarded, even though it is the only one with coordinates; HUEFS (Ormosia nitida) is kept.

If all duplicates of a block are identified just to genus, all of them go to rule 2.


Rule 2: identified by a specialist
In blocks with conflicting identifications, the records identified by one of the specialists you give are preferred, whatever the number of duplicates with other names. A specialist’s identification is more reliable than any number of identifications by others, e.g. a name repeated in the duplicates sent to several herbaria before the specimens were studied.
The specialists are given in a data frame with the columns specialist and taxon, with one row for each taxon of expertise, which can be a family, a genus or a species:
