  specialist = c("D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "H. C. Lima", "W. A. Rodrigues"),
  taxon = c("Ormosia", "Swartzia", "Leguminosae", "Myristicaceae"))

A specialist counts only in blocks with a name of their taxa, so a specialist of Swartzia does not decide between names of Ormosia. When a duplicate was identified as another genus (e.g. Ormosia and Swartzia in the same block), a specialist of any of them counts.
Families are compared with the column family (set colname_family if it has another name), also by their alternative names: Leguminosae and Fabaceae, Compositae and Asteraceae, Gramineae and Poaceae, Palmae and Arecaceae, Cruciferae and Brassicaceae, Guttiferae and Clusiaceae, Labiatae and Lamiaceae, Umbelliferae and Apiaceae.
A record counts as identified by a specialist when the specialist is in identifiedBy, also among several determiners (e.g. D. Cardoso & L. P. Queiroz).
A record without determiner (identifiedBy empty) that was collected by a specialist also counts, as specialists usually identify their own collections. The specialist can be the main collector (recordedBy) or one of the additional collectors (addCollector), e.g. A. Alves, D. Cardoso & K. Paixão, as barroso_std() keeps all additional collectors.
Names are compared by surname and first initial, so D. B. O. S. Cardoso matches D. Cardoso.

For example, if two duplicates of A. Silva 1 are identified as Ormosia arborea and two as Ormosia fastigiata, one of them by H. C. Lima, then with H. C. Lima as a specialist of Leguminosae or Ormosia, the record of Ormosia fastigiata identified by H. C. Lima is kept. Without specialists, or when the specialists disagree, the next rule applies.


Rule 3: most frequent identification
Among the remaining records, those with the name given by most duplicates are preferred.

Block 1: Ormosia arborea is given by three duplicates (MO, JBB, HUEFS) and Swartzia apetala by one (K), so K is discarded; MO, JBB and HUEFS go to rule 5.



Rule 4: equally frequent names are never chosen at random
When two or more names are still equally frequent, e.g. one duplicate as Ormosia arborea and one as Ormosia nitida, or two and two, there is no way to know which name is correct. Choosing one of them by the completeness of the records would be choosing at random, and the other identification would disappear from the data. So:

By default (rm_tied_conflicts = FALSE), the block is not reduced: all its records are kept, so you can check them, filtering them by identificationUnresolved = TRUE. This matters in taxonomic revisions and checklists, where every specimen must be included or checked, and never removed or combined at random.
With rm_tied_conflicts = TRUE, the whole block is removed. This may suit macroecological analyses of many species, where a record of uncertain identity is worse than a missing record.

In both cases, a message tells how many records and blocks were kept or removed, and why, e.g.:
barroso_flag_duplicates: 6 records of 2 blocks removed, as their duplicates are identified as different species, equally frequent, so the correct name cannot be chosen (rm_tied_conflicts = TRUE)


Rule 5: most complete record
Among the remaining records, the one with the most complete information is kept:

records with latitude and longitude are preferred;
then, records with more filled columns;
if records are still tied, the first one in the data is kept.


Block 1: MO has no coordinates and is discarded. JBB and HUEFS both have coordinates, but HUEFS also has the locality, so HUEFS 187321 is kept.

title: Detect and Flag Duplicates
text:
Summary of the rules







Step
Rule




Grouping
Same collector and collector number; or same species, collector and full date when the number is missing. Unknown collectors are never grouped.


Conflict
Different species or genera in the same block. Genus-only records do not conflict with species of the same genus.


Rule 1
Keep records identified to species rather than just to genus.


Rule 2
In conflicting blocks, keep records identified (or collected, also as additional collector, when without determiner) by the specialists of the taxa of the block, whatever the number of other names.


Rule 3
Keep records with the most frequent identification of the block.


Rule 4
When names are still equally frequent, the block is marked with identificationUnresolved = TRUE, and all its records are kept (default), or the whole block is removed with rm_tied_conflicts = TRUE.


Rule 5
Keep the record with coordinates, then with more filled columns, then the first one.

title: Detect and Flag Duplicates
text:
Best Practices

Run this step after standardizing fields with barroso_std().
Inspect the blocks with identificationConflict == TRUE before removing duplicates, as they may reveal misidentified or misspelled names.
Keep rm_duplicates = FALSE when you want to review the blocks first; the columns duplicateGroup and duplicateIdentifications make it easy to sort and filter them.
Give the specialists of your group, with their taxa of expertise, so their identifications are kept in conflicting blocks.
Run barroso_fix_names() before, so that synonyms and misspelled names are not taken as conflicts.
For taxonomic revisions and checklists, keep rm_tied_conflicts = FALSE, and check the blocks with identificationUnresolved == TRUE, which were kept with all their records.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
What is the barRoso?
barRoso is an R package for cleaning, standardizing, and reconciling plant specimen records—especially from biodiversity repositories like GBIF. It streamlines workflows for curators, researchers, and data scientists by automating the harmonization of taxonomic, geographic, and collector metadata. Optimized for reproducibility, barRoso facilitates the detection of duplicate specimens and improves data quality across herbarium datasets.


What can I use barRoso for?

Standardize collector names and associated collector numbers — a crucial step for detecting duplicate specimens across herbaria
Harmonize taxonomic and geographic fields (e.g., family, genus, locality, country)
Detect and flag potential duplicate records using cleaned metadata
Generate herbarium labels from field notebooks, including taxon authority and geolocation maps
Prepare high-quality datasets for biodiversity, floristic, and taxonomic studies



How do I install barRoso?
Follow the Get Started guide for full instructions on installing the package and its dependencies via GitHub.


Is barRoso free to use?
Yes. barRoso is open-source software licensed under the MIT License, which permits unrestricted use, modification, and distribution.


What output can barRoso generate?
While barRoso does not directly produce formatted reports, it supports:

Cleaned and standardized data frames for downstream biodiversity analysis
Visual maps in herbarium label generation
Easy integration with RMarkdown, Quarto, and Shiny for reporting and dashboards



How does barRoso work?
Unlike many packages that rely on static dictionaries to clean collector names, barRoso uses a robust set of regular expressions (regex) to dynamically identify and standardize collector patterns across datasets. This approach allows barRoso to generalize better across sources and spelling variations — even when names are inconsistently formatted. Combined with harmonization of geographic and taxonomic fields, this makes the package especially powerful for detecting duplicates and preparing data for downstream analysis.


Why doesn’t barRoso remove incomplete or inconsistent records?
Because standardization is more powerful than deletion. Many biodiversity records contain valuable metadata even when some fields are missing or messy. barRoso standardizes and flags potential problems but leaves the final decision to the user—preserving data integrity and maximizing research potential.


Who are the developers of barRoso?
Development is sponsored by JBRJ, FINEP, and CNPq. Main developer:

Domingos Cardoso (@DBOSlab)

View the code and contribute on GitHub: https://github.com/DBOSlab/barRoso


Why the name barRoso?
The name honors Graziela Maciel Barroso (1912–2003), a pioneering Brazilian botanist. It also serves as an acronym: Biodiversity Analysis and Record Reconciliation for Organizing Specimen Observations, highlighting both its mission and its deep roots in the R programming ecosystem.


Where can I report bugs or request features?
Submit issues on GitHub: barRoso Issues.


Where can I ask questions or join the community?
Visit GitHub Discussions to ask questions, share ideas, or connect with other users.

title: Format Datasets into Darwin Core
text:
Overview
Herbarium records downloaded from different portals rarely share the same column names and formats. GBIF uses Darwin Core terms such as recordedBy and decimalLatitude, while a speciesLink download may call them collector and latitude, write dates as 23/11/2011, or keep the year, month and day of identification in separate columns.
The function barroso_dwc() formats a dataset into Darwin Core column names and value formats, so records from GBIF, speciesLink, REFLORA and JABOT can be combined and standardized together. It recognizes the source of the data by itself.

title: Format Datasets into Darwin Core
text:
Usage
library(barRoso)

splink <- readxl::read_excel("speciesLink-20260409091223-0027073.xlsx", col_types = "text")

splink <- barroso_dwc(splink)
#> barroso_dwc: speciesLink format; renamed 20 columns (collector -> recordedBy,
#> collectornumber -> recordNumber, yearcollected -> year, monthcollected -> month, ...);
#> renamed 13 columns (basisofrecord -> basisOfRecord, stateprovince -> stateProvince, ...);
#> cleaned 3097 specificEpithet (e.g. "cf. platychila", "sp. 2"); created dateIdentified
#> from year, month and day of identification; added the author to 133418 scientificName;
#> took 1585 missing recordNumber from fieldNumber; created species from genus and
#> specificEpithet
The report tells what was changed. The source can also be given explicitly:
splink <- barroso_dwc(splink, source = "speciesLink")   # also "REFLORA", "JABOT", "GBIF"
You don’t need to call barroso_dwc() before barroso_cat(): it formats each source by itself before combining them.
combined <- barroso_cat(list(GBIF = gbif, speciesLink = splink), keep_source = c("GBIF", "speciesLink"))
All columns are returned as character, so the outputs of different downloads can always be combined. For example, when querying several species with plantR::rspeciesLink(), a column like coordinatePrecision may come as integer for one species and as character for another, and dplyr::bind_rows() would fail:
data_speciesLink <- lapply(targeted_taxa, function(x) {
  splink <- plantR::rspeciesLink(key = personal_key, species = x, save = FALSE)
  barroso_dwc(splink)
})
names(data_speciesLink) <- targeted_taxa
data_speciesLink <- dplyr::bind_rows(data_speciesLink, .id = "original_search")
Use as_character = FALSE to keep the original column types.

title: Flexible Column Names
text:
Overview
Herbarium datasets vary widely in how they name their columns. One dataset might label a column as estado, while another might use stateProvince or province. To make barRoso work with any data source, all standardization functions support flexible column naming.
The barroso_std() function accepts parameters such as colname_country, colname_stateProvince, colname_recordedBy, and more. These let you specify the actual column names in your input data.
This flexibility is essential when cleaning datasets from mixed sources like GBIF, speciesLink, JABOT, or SEINet.

title: Flexible Column Names
text:
Specifying Custom Column Names
Use named arguments in barroso_std() to point to your actual column names. For example:
library(barRoso)

# Assume your dataset uses "pais" and "estado" instead of "country" and "stateProvince"
df <- read.csv("raw_data.csv")

df_std <- barroso_std(df,
                      colname_country = "pais",
                      colname_stateProvince = "estado",
                      colname_recordedBy = "coletor",
                      colname_recordNumber = "numero",
                      colname_identifiedBy = "determinador",
                      colname_collectionCode = "herbario",
                      colname_institutionCode = "instituicao",
                      colname_locality = "localidade",
                      colname_family = "familia",
                      colname_genus = "genero",
                      colname_specificEpithet = "epiteto",
                      rm_duplicates = TRUE)
The standardized columns keep your names, and the original values are kept with the suffix Original, e.g. herbario and herbarioOriginal.
The individual functions accept the same arguments, e.g.:
df_std <- std_collection(df,
                         colname_collectionCode = "herbario",
                         colname_institutionCode = "instituicao",
                         rm_original_column = FALSE)

df_coords <- std_coordinates(df,
                             colname_decimalLatitude = "latitude",
                             colname_decimalLongitude = "longitude",
                             colname_country = "pais")

text:
Why This Matters

Ensures compatibility with multilingual datasets
Prevents failure due to missing or misnamed columns
Helps merge and clean records from disparate herbaria

title: Flexible Column Names
text:
Recommendations

Always check the column headers of your CSV or data frame before calling barroso_std()
Rename fields only if necessary — using this feature gives you more flexibility

This makes barRoso highly generalizable for data standardization across any herbarium or biodiversity dataset.

title: Update a Database with New Downloads
text:
Overview
A database of herbarium records is rarely finished in one go. You download the records of your group from GBIF, speciesLink, REFLORA and JABOT, standardize them with barroso_std(), remove the duplicates, and then spend weeks correcting names, localities and coordinates by hand. Months later, new records are online: newly digitized herbaria, specimens of recent expeditions, or taxa you did not download before.
Downloading everything again and running barroso_std() from scratch would bring back all records you already have, and lose all your corrections. With the argument database, barroso_std() instead adds only the new records to your corrected database:
updated <- barroso_std(new_records,
                       rm_duplicates = TRUE,
                       database = "results/Ormosia_database.xlsx")
The records of your database are not standardized again and not changed, except that new duplicates of their specimens are added to their duplicate columns. Only the new records are standardized, which is also much faster.

title: Update a Database with New Downloads
text:
The workflow

1. Build and correct your database
library(barRoso)

sources <- list(GBIF = data_gbif, speciesLink = data_speciesLink,
                REFLORA = data_reflora, JABOT = data_jabot)

data_all <- barroso_cat(sources, keep_source = c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "GBIF"))
data_all <- barroso_fix_names(data_all)
data_all <- barroso_std(data_all, rm_duplicates = TRUE)

openxlsx::write.xlsx(data_all, "results/Ormosia_database.xlsx")
Then correct the spreadsheet by hand as needed. Keep these columns, which are used to recognize the records already in the database:







Column
Used for




datasource, occurrenceID (and gbifID, if you keep it)
Records already in the database, by their identifiers (step 2)


collectionCode, catalogNumber, duplicateCatalogNumbers
Herbarium sheets already in the database (step 4)


recordedBy, recordNumber, genus, specificEpithet, year, month, day
Duplicates of the specimens of the database (step 6)


duplicate, duplicateGroup, duplicateIdentifications, duplicateCollectionCodes
Updated with the new duplicates (step 6)



You can add your own columns, e.g. notes or traits; they are kept, and empty for the new records.


2. Download the records again, and add them to the database
new_sources <- list(GBIF = new_gbif, speciesLink = new_speciesLink,
                    REFLORA = new_reflora, JABOT = new_jabot)

new_records <- barroso_cat(new_sources, keep_source = c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "GBIF"))
new_records <- barroso_fix_names(new_records)

updated <- barroso_std(new_records,
                       rm_duplicates = TRUE,
                       database = "results/Ormosia_database.xlsx")

# The new records, to be checked
subset(updated, newRecord)

openxlsx::write.xlsx(updated, "results/Ormosia_database_updated.xlsx")
Use the same arguments of barroso_cat() and barroso_std() you used to build the database (e.g. the order of keep_source), so that the new records are standardized in the same way. The database can be a data frame, or the path to an .xlsx, .csv or .rds file.

title: Update a Database with New Downloads
section: How the new records are compared with the database
text:
How the new records are compared with the database
The new records go through six steps. Each one removes the records found in the database, so the next steps only deal with the remaining ones.

Step 1: the database is read
The database is read as it is. It is not standardized again.


Step 2: records with the same identifier
Each source gives a unique identifier to each record, which stays the same when the record is downloaded again: occurrenceID, found in GBIF, REFLORA and JABOT records (GBIF also has gbifID, which is used too when kept, but is not needed). barroso_cat() keeps them, with the source of each record in datasource. New records with the same identifier of the same source as a record of the database are removed before standardizing, so most records already in the database are not standardized again.
Records without an identifier, from any source, are simply recognized by their catalog numbers in step 4. This is the case of all records of speciesLink downloads made with plantR, and of a few records of other sources, e.g. GBIF records without gbifID, or records whose identifier column was not kept in the database. barroso_cat() tells how many there are, e.g.:
barroso_cat: all records of speciesLink have no unique identifier (no column gbifID or occurrenceID); when updating a database with barroso_std(database = ...), they are compared by their catalog numbers
barroso_cat: 2 of 15841 records of GBIF have no unique identifier (gbifID or occurrenceID); when updating a database with barroso_std(database = ...), they are compared by their catalog numbers


Step 3: the other new records are standardized
As usual: collectors, determiners, herbaria, catalog numbers, places, names, types and dates.


Step 4: herbarium sheets already in the database
New records whose herbarium and catalog number, e.g. MO 2839102, are already in the database are removed, as they are the same herbarium sheet. The catalog numbers of the database are taken from catalogNumber and from duplicateCatalogNumbers, which keeps the catalog numbers of the duplicates removed with rm_duplicates = TRUE.
This is why duplicateCatalogNumbers matters. When you built the database, the duplicate of D. Cardoso 1350 at K was removed, and only its record at MO was kept, with MO 2839102 | K000123 in duplicateCatalogNumbers. The record at K is downloaded again, with a gbifID that is not in the database, but its catalog number is found in duplicateCatalogNumbers, so it is not added again.
Records without catalog number are compared by all their standardized fields: herbarium, collector, number, name, date and place. A record like E. Ule s.n. (US) of Ormosia arborea, without number, date or catalog number, is removed when the database has the same record.


Step 5: duplicates among the new records
Duplicates are flagged among the new records, and removed with rm_duplicates = TRUE, as described in Detect and Flag Duplicates, with specialists and rm_tied_conflicts if given.


Step 6: duplicates of the specimens of the database
A new record can be a new herbarium sheet of a specimen already in the database, e.g. a duplicate of L. P. Queiroz 200 at NY, newly digitized. It is found by the same collector and number (or the same species, collector and date, without number), also when the collector is written in another way, e.g. L. Queiroz in the database and L. P. Queiroz in the new record, with the same date or municipality (see the same collector written in other ways). New records not in the database also get the most complete name of their collector in the database. Then:

Its herbarium, catalog number and name are added to the duplicate columns of the record of the database: duplicateCollectionCodes becomes HUEFS | NY, duplicateCatalogNumbers becomes HUEFS1 | NY555.
With rm_duplicates = TRUE, it is removed, as the specimen is already in the database. With rm_duplicates = FALSE, it is kept, with the same duplicateGroup of the record of the database.
If it has another name, e.g. Ormosia arborea for a specimen of Ormosia fastigiata in the database, identificationConflict becomes TRUE, so that you can check it, but the name of the database is kept, as it may have been corrected by you.

Blocks of duplicates of the new records are numbered after those of the database, so duplicateGroup never mixes blocks.

The result has all records of the database, followed by the new records, sorted by species, collector and number, with the column newRecord:







newRecord

TRUE

The messages tell what happened in each step, e.g. for Ormosia, when a database of 6,755 records was updated with the same four sources downloaded again, plus 300 GBIF records that were not in the first download:
barroso_std: database with 6755 records
barroso_std: 3773 of 11631 new records already in the database (same gbifID or occurrenceID of the same datasource) removed; 5443 new records without identifier are compared by their catalog numbers
barroso_std: 6429 of 6521 new records of herbarium sheets already in the database removed (6374 by catalogNumber or duplicateCatalogNumbers, 55 without catalog number, with the same fields)
barroso_std: 46 new records are duplicates of 46 records of the database, added to their duplicate columns and removed

All 41 added records were among the 300 GBIF records left out of the first download. Of these 300, 224 were removed by barroso_cat(), as their herbaria come from sources before GBIF in keep_source, and of the other 76, 41 were new specimens, and most of the rest new sheets of specimens already in the database. The records of the database were unchanged, except the duplicate columns of 42 of them. The update took a few seconds, as only 6,521 records were standardized.
When nothing is new, the database is returned as it is:
barroso_std: no new records to add to the database

title: Update a Database with New Downloads
text:
Tips

Keep the columns datasource and occurrenceID in your database (gbifID is not needed), even if you select just some columns to work with. Without them, all new records are standardized and compared only by their catalog numbers and fields, which is slower and misses records without catalog number whose fields were corrected by hand.
Keep duplicateCatalogNumbers and duplicateCollectionCodes: they tell which herbarium sheets were removed as duplicates.
Check the new records with subset(updated, newRecord), and the records of the database with new conflicts with subset(updated, !newRecord & identificationConflict).
Save the updated database with a new name, so that you can go back to the previous one.

title: Standardize Specimen Records
text:
Overview
The barroso_std() function is the primary tool in the barRoso package for performing full data cleaning and standardization of biodiversity specimen records. It is designed to process raw data from herbaria, virtual repositories, and field collections, ensuring harmonized fields across taxonomic, geographic, and collector-related information.

title: Standardize Specimen Records
text:
Key Features

Normalize collector names and collection numbers
Normalize determiner names (identifiedBy)
Standardize geographic fields like country, state, and locality
Harmonize taxonomic names including family, genus, and species
Clean and normalize type status
Fix the day, month and year of collection, e.g. days and months in the wrong columns
Optionally remove unvouchered or duplicate records
Support for multilingual column names (e.g., Portuguese, Spanish)

title: Standardize Specimen Records
text:
Usage
library(barRoso)

df <- read.csv("raw_herbarium_data.csv")

standardized_df <- barroso_std(df,
                               unvouchered = TRUE,
                               delunkcoll = FALSE,
                               flag_missid = TRUE,
                               flag_duplicates = TRUE,
                               rm_duplicates = FALSE,
                               index_herbariorum = TRUE,
                               colname_recordedBy = "recordedBy",
                               colname_recordNumber = "recordNumber",
                               colname_identifiedBy = "identifiedBy",
                               colname_country = "country",
                               colname_stateProvince = "stateProvince",
                               colname_county = "county",
                               colname_municipality = "municipality",
                               colname_locality = "locality",
                               colname_collectionCode = "collectionCode",
                               colname_institutionCode = "institutionCode",

                               colname_family = "family",

title: Standardize Specimen Records
text:
Arguments

...: A data frame or list of data frames with raw biodiversity records
unvouchered: Remove records of wood, seed, fruit, pollen and spirit collections (e.g. INPAw, INPA-Carpoteca, BHZBcarpo), and observations without a specimen (basisOfRecord like HUMAN_OBSERVATION), before the herbarium codes are standardized
delunkcoll: Optionally delete records with unknown collectors
flag_duplicates, rm_duplicates: Detect and optionally remove duplicates
specialists, rm_tied_conflicts: How duplicates with conflicting identifications are kept, see Detect and Flag Duplicates
flag_specialists: Flag the records identified by the specialists, see Flag Identifications by Specialists
match_collectors: Deep search across the whole data for the same collector written in other ways, e.g. L. Queiroz and L. P. Queiroz with the same number and date or municipality, see Detect and Flag Duplicates (default: TRUE)
database: A database already standardized, to which the new records are added, see Update a Database with New Downloads
index_herbariorum: Check collection codes against the API of Index Herbariorum, always keeping the original codes (default: TRUE)
rm_original_column: Remove original (uncleaned) fields after standardization

title: Standardize Specimen Records
text:
Places
Countries, states, counties and municipalities are standardized with std_place(), e.g. BRASIL into Brazil and BA into Bahia. Words for municipality are removed from county and municipality, leaving just the name, e.g. Manaus Mun., Mun. de Castelo and Município de Mucugê into Manaus, Castelo and Mucugê. Country codes become names, e.g. BR and GY into Brazil and Guyana. Missing countries are taken from the Brazilian state (e.g. Bahia), from a country name at the start or end of the locality (e.g. Rio Negro, Brasil), or from other records with the same state and county (e.g. Amazonas, Manaus); names shared by several countries, like the state Amazonas alone, are left empty. Missing municipalities are taken from the county, as GBIF keeps the municipalities of Brazil in county. Localities all in upper case get just the first letter of each word in upper case, e.g. ESTR. UBAITUBA / MARÁU AO KM 54 . into Estr. Ubaituba/Maráu ao Km 54., keeping prepositions in lowercase and road codes (BR-316), acronyms (ESALQ) and compass points (10 Km NE de) in upper case.
The final data frame is sorted by species, recordedBy and recordNumber. All records of a block of duplicates stay together under the most frequent name of the block, e.g. a duplicate identified as Ormosia ruddiana goes with its three duplicates identified as Ormosia amazonica, in the place of the latter species.
The function barroso_std() does not check geographic coordinates. Use std_coordinates() for that.

title: Fix Species Names
text:
Overview
Herbarium records of the same species often come with different names: misspellings (Ormosia excelsea), old spellings (Ormosia timböensis) and synonyms (Ormosia glazioviana). Before standardizing large datasets and flagging duplicates, these names should be harmonized, so that duplicates identified with different names of the same species are recognized, and the records of each species are kept together.
barroso_fix_names() updates misspelled names and synonyms into accepted names, using:

the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) of Plants of the World Online as a global backbone, through the package expowo;
by default, the Flora e Funga do Brasil (FFB), through the package floraR, which is preferred for the names it has.

It is run after barroso_cat() and before barroso_std(). This order matters when removing duplicates: duplicates of the same specimen identified with a synonym and its accepted name, or with a misspelled name, would otherwise be taken as conflicting identifications, and could even create false ties of names that cannot be resolved (see Detect and Flag Duplicates).

text:
Installation
expowo and floraR are needed only for this function:
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("DBOSlab/expowo")
remotes::install_github("DBOSlab/floraR")
The first use downloads the WCVP (by expowo) and the FFB dataset (by floraR), which are then kept in cache folders for the next uses.

title: Fix Species Names
text:
How It Works

1. Each name is searched once
Binomials are built from genus and specificEpithet, and each unique binomial is searched just once, so large datasets are fixed quickly. Names without a specific epithet (e.g. Ormosia, Ormosia sp.) are not searched.


2. Flora e Funga do Brasil
With flora_brasil = TRUE, all names are searched at once with floraR::flora_search(), which also corrects misspellings of the specific epithet. The FFB dataset is downloaded once into the barRoso cache folder, so nothing is written to your working folder.


3. World Checklist of Vascular Plants
All names of the families in the data (and of the families of their genera in FFB) are read at once with expowo::powoSpecies(family, synonyms = TRUE). Names are first matched exactly, and misspelled names are matched to the closest name of the same genus, with a relative distance of the specific epithet up to max_distance. Misspelled genera are matched in the same way. Homonyms with different accepted names, and ties between misspelled names, are left as they are (ambiguous).


4. FFB first, then WCVP
Names found in FFB follow FFB, and the other names follow WCVP. A misspelling found in FFB is not taken for a name found as it is in WCVP, as names of other countries are often close to Brazilian names (e.g. Ormosia panamensis and Ormosia paraensis).


5. The records are updated
When a name is updated, family, genus, specificEpithet, and when present species, scientificName, scientificNameAuthorship and taxonName, get the accepted name, and infraspecificEpithet becomes NA. Accepted infraspecific names are reduced to the binomial. The family is also updated for accepted names in another family (e.g. Leguminosae into Fabaceae).
Three columns are added after specificEpithet:







Column
Content




taxonOriginal
The binomial (or genus) before the fix


taxonStatus
accepted, synonym, misspelled, misspelled synonym, ambiguous, not found, or NA for names without specific epithet


taxonSource
FFB or WCVP

Check the names with taxonStatus equal to not found or ambiguous, which are left as they are.
Use flora_brasil = FALSE for datasets of other regions, so that all names follow WCVP.
Use vascular_only = TRUE to keep just vascular plants when working with all records of a herbarium.

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Overview
When working with plant specimen data from multiple biodiversity repositories (e.g., GBIF, JABOT, speciesLink), users often encounter overlapping records across sources. barRoso offers the barroso_cat() function to merge and harmonize these datasets, keeping the records of each herbarium from a single source, chosen by an order of priority of the sources.
This article demonstrates how to:

Merge multiple data sources into a unified data frame
Combine raw speciesLink downloads with GBIF downloads
Keep each herbarium from the first source that has it, in your order of priority

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Function: barroso_cat()
combined_df <- barroso_cat(
  list_sources = list(
    GBIF = gbif_data,
    speciesLink = splink_data,
    JABOT = jabot_data
  ),
  keep_source = c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "GBIF"),
  index_herbariorum = TRUE
)

title: Compare Herbarium Sources
text:
Arguments

list_sources: A named list of data frames, one per biodiversity source. The names (e.g. GBIF, speciesLink) must be unique, as they are used to identify the source of each record.
keep_source: The names of all sources of list_sources, in order of priority, e.g. c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "GBIF"). It is required, as the same herbarium is often in several sources. The herbaria of each source are removed from the sources after it, so each herbarium is kept from the first source that has it (see below).
index_herbariorum: If TRUE (the default), the herbarium acronyms of each source are checked against the API of Index Herbariorum before comparing the sources. Use FALSE to work offline.

text:
Example
library(barRoso)

# Load datasets downloaded from GBIF and speciesLink
gbif <- read.csv("gbif.csv")
splink <- read.csv("speciesLink.csv", fileEncoding = "latin1")

# Merge, keeping the herbaria of speciesLink first, and from GBIF only the others
combined_df <- barroso_cat(
  list_sources = list(
    GBIF = gbif,
    speciesLink = splink
  ),
  keep_source = c("speciesLink", "GBIF")
)

table(combined_df$datasource)

The REFLORA collection of RB is fed by JABOT, so the same RB specimens are often found in both sources, and also in GBIF. With JABOT first, they are kept just once, from JABOT.


3. Herbarium acronyms are standardized in each source
The same herbarium is often written differently in each source, e.g. MO-Duplicates or MOBOT_BR in speciesLink and MO in GBIF. So, before comparing the sources, the acronyms in collectionCode of each source are standardized with std_collection(), and checked against Index Herbariorum by default:

The original codes are kept in collectionCodeOriginal. So unvouchered collections like INPA-Carpoteca, whose acronym becomes INPA, are still removed later by barroso_std(). Index Herbariorum is downloaded once for all sources, and if it cannot be reached, a warning is given and the acronyms are standardized with the regular expressions only.


4. Overlapping herbaria are kept from a single source
Overlapping herbaria are detected with collectionCode, and the sources are compared one after the other, in the order of keep_source. With keep_source = c("JABOT", "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "GBIF"):

The herbaria of JABOT are removed from speciesLink, REFLORA and GBIF.
The remaining herbaria of speciesLink are removed from REFLORA and GBIF.
The remaining herbaria of REFLORA are removed from GBIF.

So no herbarium is kept from two sources, and GBIF adds only the herbaria that are in none of the other sources. A message tells how many records and herbaria were removed from each source, and why, e.g. removing 845 records of 70 herbaria from speciesLink also present in JABOT. Duplicates among different herbaria (e.g. the same collection at RB and K) are then flagged with barroso_flag_duplicates().


5. Identifiers of the records are kept
The identifier of each record in its source is kept as it is: occurrenceID in GBIF, REFLORA and JABOT (and gbifID in GBIF), with the source in datasource. They are used to find the records already in a database when it is updated with new downloads, see Update a Database with New Downloads. Records without a unique identifier, from any source, are compared by their catalog numbers instead, and a message tells how many there are, e.g. all records of speciesLink have no unique identifier (no column gbifID or occurrenceID), or 2 of 15841 records of GBIF have no unique identifier (gbifID or occurrenceID).


6. Columns are aligned

Columns missing in some sources are filled with NA.
Columns with different types across sources (e.g. year as numbers in GBIF and as text in speciesLink) are combined as text, instead of failing.
A new column datasource stores the source of each record (e.g. "GBIF", "speciesLink").

title: barRoso
text:
Graziela Maciel Barroso
Graziela Maciel Barroso (1912–2003) was one of Brazil’s most influential botanists, with a 58-year career at the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden. She specialized in plant taxonomy and morphology, shaping how generations of scientists understand and classify Brazil’s flora. Her work was instrumental in developing identification keys and guides used in herbaria across Brazil and abroad.
She authored the landmark three-volume Sistemática de Angiospermas do Brasil (1978–1986), still a cornerstone of botanical education, as well as Frutos e Sementes – Morfologia Aplicada à Sistemática de Dicotiledôneas (1999). Beyond her scientific contributions, she was a committed educator and mentor, and a courageous advocate for science and democracy during Brazil’s military dictatorship.
Barroso remained professionally active until her passing at age 92. A month before her death, she was elected to the Brazilian Academy of Sciences, a distinction awarded posthumously.

title: News
text:
Initial Release
The first official release of the barRoso R package — a comprehensive toolkit for standardizing, harmonizing, and preparing plant specimen records for research and reconciliation.

Highlights

barroso_std(): Unified function to clean and standardize herbarium records across multiple fields (collector, geography, taxonomy, etc.).
barroso_flag_duplicates(): Flag potential duplicate specimens across herbaria using metadata patterns.
barroso_cat(): Combine and reconcile specimen records from multiple virtual herbaria (e.g., GBIF, SEINet, REFLORA, JABOT, speciesLink).
barroso_labels(): Generate printable herbarium labels from cleaned fieldbook data, with embedded maps and taxonomic authority retrieval.
Standardize collector names and collection numbers using regex-based parsing
Harmonize taxonomic, geographic, and temporal fields
Flag and remove potential duplicates across herbarium records
Generate herbarium labels from fieldbook data
Integrate with external taxonomic databases (e.g., LCVP, WFO)
Prepare large-scale biodiversity datasets for publication and analysis
Optimized for datasets from REFLORA, speciesLink, and JABOT.
Supports integration with tidyverse workflows for downstream analyses.
Test coverage >95%, continuous integration via GitHub Actions.



Philosophy
Unlike other tools that aggressively clean (and discard) records, barRoso focuses on standardization first — ensuring that all specimens, even misidentified or ambiguous ones, remain usable and discoverable. Standardization also enables better duplicate detection and data reconciliation without losing valuable information.

title: std_types

barRoso::std_types()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the typeStatus column in biodiversity datasets, addressing inconsistencies in type designations. It removes irrelevant entries, harmonizes formatting, and optionally fills missing values if present in other duplicate records (assumed to be handled outside this function).


Details
This function is used internally in the barRoso package to prepare type status data for reconciliation and label generation. It corrects known placeholder or non-type entries (e.g. “Fotografia do Tipo”, “NOTATYPE”, “Epítipo”) and simplifies terms like "sim -" to ensure clean type labels.
The same type designation written in English, Latin or Portuguese, and in any case, is converted into the lowercase Darwin Core term in English, e.g. "ISOTYPE", "Isotypus" and "isótipo" into "isotype", "Parátipo" into "paratype", and "isosintipo" into "isosyntype". A taxon name after the term is kept, e.g. "ISOTYPUS of Ormosia amazonica Ducke" into "isotype of Ormosia amazonica Ducke".


Arguments







Argument

A data frame containing type designation records.


colname_typeStatus
Name of the column holding type status information (default: "typeStatus").


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, the original column is removed after cleaning (default: TRUE).

A data frame with a standardized typeStatus column. If rm_original_column = FALSE, the original values are preserved in a column named typeStatusOriginal.

df <- read.csv("specimens.csv")
df_clean <- std_types(df,

title: barroso_flag_duplicates
text:
barRoso::barroso_flag_duplicates()


Description
Identifies and optionally removes duplicate herbarium specimen records based on collector name and number, or—when the number is missing—by species name, collector and date. Duplicates are grouped into blocks, and blocks with conflicting identifications are highlighted. The herbaria and catalog numbers of all duplicates are stored together, so no information is lost when duplicates are removed.


Details
This function is part of the internal workflow of the barRoso package, supporting record reconciliation and dataset cleaning. Duplicates are records with the same collector (recordedBy) and collector number (recordNumber). For records without collector number, duplicates must share the species name, the collector and the full collection date (year, month, day). Records with unknown collector (NA or "Unknown") are never treated as duplicates.
The following columns are added after the collector number:

duplicate: TRUE for records belonging to a block of duplicates.
duplicateGroup: an identifier of each block of duplicates.
identificationConflict: TRUE when the duplicates of a block are identified as different species (e.g. "Ormosia arborea" and "Ormosia fastigiata") or genera. A duplicate identified just to genus (e.g. "Ormosia") does not conflict with a complete name of the same genus. Names are compared exactly, so spelling variants (e.g. "Ormosia trifoliata" and "Ormosia trifoliolata") are also flagged as conflicts, which helps finding misspelled names.
identificationUnresolved: TRUE for the records of blocks with conflicting identifications whose name cannot be chosen by the rules below, as their names are equally frequent (e.g. two duplicates as "Ormosia arborea" and two as "Ormosia fastigiata"), even after specialists. These blocks need checking: with rm_duplicates = TRUE and rm_tied_conflicts = FALSE, all their records are kept. FALSE for the other duplicates, and NA for records that are not duplicates.
duplicateIdentifications: all names found in the block, e.g. "Ormosia arborea | Ormosia fastigiata".
duplicateCollectionCodes: all herbaria of the block, e.g. "MO | JBB".
duplicateCatalogNumbers: all catalog numbers of the block with their herbarium, e.g. "MO 2839102 | JBB 13548".

The specific epithet is taken from specificEpithet or, when missing, from a binomial in the column species (as in GBIF downloads).
When rm_duplicates = TRUE, one record per block is kept, chosen as follows:

Records identified to species are preferred over those identified just to genus.
In blocks with conflicting identifications, the records identified by one of the specialists are preferred, whatever the number of duplicates with other names, when the taxon of expertise of the specialist includes one of the names of the block. A record without determiner (identifiedBy) that was collected by a specialist, as main (recordedBy) or additional collector (addCollector), counts as identified by the specialist.
Among them, records with the most frequent identification in the block are preferred (e.g. the name given by two duplicates rather than by one).
When two or more names are still equally frequent (e.g. two duplicates as "Ormosia arborea" and two as "Ormosia fastigiata"), it is not possible to know which name is correct, so the block is not reduced: all its records are kept, to be checked, as needed in taxonomic revisions and checklists. With rm_tied_conflicts = TRUE, as may suit macroecological analyses, the whole block is removed instead, and a message tells how many records and blocks were removed and why.
Among the records with the chosen name, records with latitude and longitude, and then records with more filled columns, are preferred. If records are still tied, the first one in the data is kept.

The kept record still has identificationConflict and all the names, herbaria and catalog numbers of its block, so conflicting identifications remain visible after removing the duplicates.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame with biodiversity specimen records.


rm_duplicates
Logical; if TRUE, keeps just one record per block of duplicates (default: FALSE).


specialists
Optional data frame with the columns specialist and taxon, one row for each specialist and taxon of expertise, which can be a family (e.g. "Myristicaceae", all genera and species of the family), a genus (e.g. "Ormosia") or a species (e.g. "Ormosia arborea"), e.g. data.frame(specialist = c("D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "H. C. Lima"), taxon = c("Ormosia", "Swartzia", "Leguminosae")). With rm_duplicates = TRUE, in blocks with conflicting identifications that include a name of their taxa, the records identified by them (or collected by them, also as additional collectors, when without determiner) are preferred. Names are compared by surname and first initial, so "D. B. O. S. Cardoso" matches "D. Cardoso", and families by their alternative names too, e.g. "Leguminosae" and "Fabaceae" (default: NULL).


rm_tied_conflicts
Logical; with rm_duplicates = TRUE, if TRUE, blocks whose conflicting names are equally frequent, even after specialists, are removed entirely. If FALSE, all their records are kept (default: FALSE).


colname_recordedBy
Column name for the collector (default: "recordedBy").


colname_recordNumber
Column name for the collector number (default: "recordNumber").


colname_genus
Column name for the genus (default: "genus").


colname_specificEpithet
Column name for the specific epithet (default: "specificEpithet").


colname_identifiedBy
Column name for the determiner (default: "identifiedBy").


colname_addCollector
Column name for the additional collectors (default: "addCollector").


colname_family
Column name for the family, compared with the families in specialists (default: "family").

Column name for the herbarium acronym (default: "collectionCode").

Column name for the catalog number (default: "catalogNumber").


colname_decimalLatitude
Column name for latitude (default: "decimalLatitude").


colname_decimalLongitude
Column name for longitude (default: "decimalLongitude").





Value
A data frame with the duplicate columns described above. If rm_duplicates = TRUE, only one record per block of duplicates is kept.


Examples
df <- read.csv("herbarium_data.csv")
df_flagged <- barroso_flag_duplicates(df)

# Blocks of duplicates with conflicting identifications
df_flagged[df_flagged$identificationConflict %in% TRUE, ]

df_clean <- barroso_flag_duplicates(df, rm_duplicates = TRUE)

# Identifications of specialists first, and tied conflicts removed
df_clean <- barroso_flag_duplicates(df, rm_duplicates = TRUE,
                                    specialists = data.frame(
                                      specialist = c("D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "H. C. Lima"),
                                      taxon = c("Ormosia", "Leguminosae")),
                                    rm_tied_conflicts = TRUE)

title: barroso_flag_specialists
text:
barRoso::barroso_flag_specialists()


Description
Flags the herbarium records whose identifications were given by specialists of their taxa, and so are probably accurate, or keeps just these records, e.g. to build a dataset of reliable identifications for distribution maps, niche models or checklists. The specialists are given in a data frame with their taxa of expertise, as in barroso_flag_duplicates().


Details
A record is flagged when the name of a specialist is in identifiedBy (also among several determiners, e.g. "D. Cardoso & L. P. Queiroz"), and the family, genus or species of the record is among the taxa of expertise of the specialist. Names of people are compared by surname and first initial, so "D. B. O. S. Cardoso" matches "D. Cardoso", and families also by their alternative names, e.g. Leguminosae and Fabaceae.
Two more kinds of records are flagged, as told in specialistEvidence:

"identifiedBy": identified by the specialist.
"recordedBy": without determiner, but collected by the specialist, as main (recordedBy) or additional collector (addCollector), as specialists usually identify their own collections.
"duplicate": a duplicate of the same specimen (same duplicateGroup of barroso_flag_duplicates()) with the same name was identified or collected by the specialist, e.g. the duplicate at MO of a specimen identified by the specialist at RB. This needs the columns of barroso_flag_duplicates(), so flag the duplicates before removing them, as done by barroso_std() with flag_specialists = TRUE.

The best results come from a database standardized with barroso_std(), where the names of collectors and determiners, and the families, are already standardized.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame with herbarium records, preferably standardized with barroso_std().


specialists
A data frame with the columns specialist and taxon, one row for each specialist and taxon of expertise, which can be a family (e.g. "Myristicaceae"), a genus (e.g. "Ormosia") or a species (e.g. "Ormosia arborea").


filter
Logical; if TRUE, only the records identified by the specialists are returned (default: FALSE).


colname_identifiedBy
Column name for the determiner (default: "identifiedBy").


colname_recordedBy
Column name for the collector (default: "recordedBy").


colname_addCollector
Column name for the additional collectors (default: "addCollector").


colname_family
Column name for the family (default: "family").


colname_genus
Column name for the genus (default: "genus").


colname_specificEpithet
Column name for the specific epithet (default: "specificEpithet").





Value
The data frame with three new columns: specialistIdentification (TRUE for the records identified by the specialists), specialistName (the specialist, as written in specialists, or several separated by " | ") and specialistEvidence ("identifiedBy", "recordedBy" or "duplicate"). With filter = TRUE, only the records with specialistIdentification = TRUE.


Examples
specialists <- data.frame(
  specialist = c("D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "D. B. O. S. Cardoso", "H. C. Lima"),
  taxon = c("Ormosia", "Swartzia", "Leguminosae"))

# Flag the records identified by the specialists
df <- barroso_flag_specialists(df, specialists)
table(df$specialistEvidence)

# Keep just these records
reliable <- barroso_flag_specialists(df, specialists, filter = TRUE)

title: barroso_dwc
text:
barRoso::barroso_dwc()


Description
Formats a dataset of herbarium records into Darwin Core column names and value formats, so that records downloaded from different sources, such as GBIF, speciesLink, REFLORA and JABOT, can be combined and standardized together.


Details
The source of the dataset is recognized from its columns and values, or can be given in source. Then:

Columns named as Darwin Core terms in other cases, e.g. recordedby or decimallatitude, are renamed into the terms, e.g. recordedBy and decimalLatitude, for any source.
speciesLink: the columns of the older speciesLink format are renamed into Darwin Core terms, e.g. collector into recordedBy, collectornumber into recordNumber, latitude into decimalLatitude, and species (just the epithet) into specificEpithet; spp (the binomial) becomes species, as in GBIF. The year, month and day of identification become dateIdentified; the author is added to scientificName; dates like "23/11/2011" become "2011-11-23"; and a missing recordNumber is taken from fieldNumber.
REFLORA (as returned by refloraR): the determiner "Administrador" (the system user, given to most records) becomes NA; dates like "11/10/2006" become "2006-10-11"; type status in Latin like "ISOTYPUS" becomes "isotype"; and the institution of RB becomes "JBRJ", as in GBIF and JABOT.
JABOT (as returned by jabotR): dates like "2008-9-26" or "22/4/2020" become "2008-09-26" and "2020-04-22".
GBIF: downloads are already in Darwin Core, so only the column names are checked.

In all sources, a binomial species column is created from genus and specificEpithet when missing, as in GBIF downloads. Columns that are not Darwin Core terms are kept unchanged.
By default, all columns are returned as character. Downloads of the same source may otherwise have different column types, e.g. coordinatePrecision as integer in a species with values and as character in a species without them, as in the speciesLink API used by plantR::rspeciesLink(), and then they cannot be combined with dplyr::bind_rows().
barroso_cat() runs this function on each source before combining them.


Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame of biodiversity records.


source
The source of the records: "auto" (default) to recognize it from the data, or one of "speciesLink", "REFLORA", "JABOT" or "GBIF".


as_character
Logical; if TRUE (default), all columns are returned as character, so the outputs of different downloads can always be combined.


verbose
Logical; if TRUE, reports the source and what was changed.





Value
The data frame with Darwin Core column names and value formats.


Examples
splink <- data.frame(collector = "Queiroz, L. P.", collectornumber = "1350",
                     collectioncode = "HUEFS", genus = "Ormosia", species = "arborea",
                     scientificname = "Ormosia arborea",
                     scientificnameauthor = "(Vell.) Harms",
                     yearidentified = "2005", monthidentified = "3",
                     dayidentified = NA, latitude = "-12.97", longitude = "-38.5")
barroso_dwc(splink)

title: std_recordedBy
text:
barRoso::std_recordedBy()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the recordedBy and recordNumber fields in biodiversity collection data, consolidating collector names and removing inconsistencies across herbarium records. The function identifies and formats collector initials, extracts main collector names, and handles multilingual and complex name structures including multiple collectors, Asian unicode names, and Brazilian surname conventions.


Details
This function is part of the barRoso package. It supports reconciliation of biodiversity records, especially for resolving collector name discrepancies across duplicate specimens. A new column addCollector is created when multiple collectors are detected, storing secondary collectors as "et al.". Original columns can be preserved or overwritten.
Specifically, this function performs extensive string cleaning including:

Converting Chinese names written as unicode escapes (e.g. "<U+674E><U+5149><U+7167>") into abbreviated Latin names, as Chinese authors cite themselves (e.g. "G. Z. Li")
Parsing and normalizing collector names split by &, and, e, y, ;, |, etc.
Handling cases of one, two, or more collectors
Cleaning spacing, punctuation, and known collector aliases
Adding standardized initials or removing redundant suffixes (e.g., “et al.”)



Arguments







Argument
Description




df
A data frame containing biodiversity records.


colname_recordedBy
Column name for the main collector (default: “recordedBy”).


colname_recordNumber
Column name for the collector number (default: “recordNumber”).


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, original columns are removed after cleaning. If FALSE, they are retained with *Original suffixes (default: FALSE).





Value
A data frame with cleaned and harmonized collector name fields. A new column addCollector is added where additional collectors are identified.


Examples
df <- read.csv("herbarium_records.csv")
df_clean <- std_recordedBy(df,
                           colname_recordedBy = "coletor",
                           colname_recordNumber = "num_coleta",
                           rm_original_column = FALSE)

title: barroso_std
text:
barRoso::barroso_std()


Description
A wrapper function that performs integrated cleaning and standardization of biodiversity collection records using the barRoso package. This includes harmonizing taxonomic, geographic, collector, and type status information, as well as flagging or removing unvouchered and duplicate specimens. Determiner names in identifiedBy are standardized with the same rules of collector names.


Details
This function orchestrates several std_* functions from the barRoso package to clean records from virtual herbaria and biodiversity portals. It handles multilingual field names, missing data, inconsistent formatting, and dataset chunking for large inputs. The function also detects and optionally removes duplicate records and specimens lacking voucher information.
The same collector written in other ways
After standardizing, the same collector can still be written in other ways, e.g. "L. Queiroz" and "L. P. Queiroz", which may be two people with the same collector number by chance, e.g. Luis Queiroz and Luciano Paganucci de Queiroz. So, with match_collectors = TRUE, a deep search is made across the whole data (not in chunks) for records with the same first initial, surname and collector number, but written in other ways. Compound surnames are compared in the same form, e.g. "A. Delgado-Salinas", "A. Delgado Salinas" and "A. D. Salinas" all as initials A D and surname Salinas. A record gets the most complete name (with more initials, then the longest, e.g. "A. Delgado-Salinas") only when:

its initials are among those of the complete name, with the same first initial, e.g. "L." in "L. P.", but not "L. M." in "L. P.";
it has the same date (day, month and year) or the same municipality of a record with the complete name, which shows that they are the same collection;
when several complete names fit, the one that agrees the most with the record is chosen, with 4 points for the same full date, 2 for the same year and month, 1 for the same year and 1 for the same municipality, e.g. "E. H. A. Rodrigues" of the same date and municipality rather than "E. M. A. Rodrigues" of the same municipality, for "E. A. Rodrigues". When different people agree as much, e.g. "L. Queiroz" with "L. P. Queiroz" and "L. M. Queiroz", the record is kept.

Updating a database
With database, new downloads are added to a database already standardized by barroso_std(), e.g. after duplicates were removed and records were corrected by hand, without standardizing it again and without losing the corrections:

New records already in the database are removed by their identifiers, the same occurrenceID (or gbifID, when present) of the same datasource.
The other new records are standardized as usual.
New records whose herbarium and catalog number, e.g. "MO 2839102", are in the database, in catalogNumber or among the duplicates of its records (duplicateCatalogNumbers), are removed, as they are the same herbarium sheet.
Duplicates are flagged (and removed, with rm_duplicates = TRUE) among the new records.
New records that are duplicates of a record of the database (same collector and number) are added to its duplicate columns, e.g. their herbaria and catalog numbers to duplicateCollectionCodes and duplicateCatalogNumbers, and, with rm_duplicates = TRUE, removed. A different name sets identificationConflict, but the name of the database is kept.

The records of the database are not changed, except their duplicate columns in step 5. The result has the records of the database and the new records, with the column newRecord (TRUE for the new records), so that they can be checked.
The final data frame is sorted by species, recordedBy and recordNumber. All records of a block of duplicates stay together under the name of the block, which is the most frequent name among its duplicates. For example, a duplicate identified as "Ormosia ruddiana" goes together with its three duplicates identified as "Ormosia amazonica", in the place of the latter species.


Arguments







Argument
Description




…
Input data frame containing raw biodiversity records.


unvouchered
Logical; if TRUE, remove records of wood, seed, fruit, pollen and spirit collections (e.g. "INPAw", "INPA-Carpoteca"), and observations without a specimen (basisOfRecord like "HUMAN_OBSERVATION") (default: TRUE).


delunkcoll
Logical; if TRUE, removes records with unknown or missing collectors (default: FALSE).


flag_missid
Reserved for future use. Currently not implemented.


flag_duplicates
Logical; if TRUE, flags duplicates with a logical column (default: TRUE).


rm_duplicates
Logical; if TRUE, removes duplicate specimens (default: FALSE).


specialists
Optional data frame with the columns specialist and taxon (a family, genus or species of expertise), e.g. data.frame(specialist = "D. B. O. S. Cardoso", taxon = "Leguminosae"), whose identifications are preferred when removing duplicates with conflicting identifications. See barroso_flag_duplicates() (default: NULL).


flag_specialists
Logical; if TRUE, the records identified by the specialists are flagged in the columns specialistIdentification, specialistName and specialistEvidence, before duplicates are removed, so that a record kept from a block of duplicates is flagged when one of its duplicates with the same name was identified by a specialist. See barroso_flag_specialists() (default: FALSE).


rm_tied_conflicts
Logical; with rm_duplicates = TRUE, if TRUE, blocks of duplicates whose conflicting names are equally frequent are removed entirely; if FALSE, all their records are kept. See barroso_flag_duplicates() (default: FALSE).


database
Optional data frame, or path to an .xlsx, .csv or .rds file, with records already standardized by barroso_std(), to which the new records are added. See Details (default: NULL).


match_collectors
Logical; if TRUE, the same collector written in other ways across the whole data, e.g. "L. Queiroz" and "L. P. Queiroz", or "A. D. Salinas", "A. Delgado Salinas" and "A. Delgado-Salinas", gets the most complete name, before duplicates are found. See Details (default: TRUE).


index_herbariorum
Logical; if TRUE, checks collection codes against the API of Index Herbariorum, always keeping the original codes. See std_collection(). Use FALSE to work offline (default: TRUE).


colname_recordedBy
Column name for collector names.


colname_recordNumber
Column name for collector number.


colname_identifiedBy
Column name for determiner names. The column is standardized with std_identifiedBy() only when present in the data.


colname_continent
Column name for continent.


colname_country
Column name for country.


colname_stateProvince
Column name for state/province.


colname_county
Column name for county.


colname_municipality
Column name for municipality.


colname_locality
Column name for locality.


colname_collectionCode
Column name for collection code.


colname_institutionCode
Column name for institution code.


colname_typeStatus
Column name for type status.


colname_family
Column name for family.


colname_genus
Column name for genus.


colname_specificEpithet
Column name for specific epithet.


rm_original_column
Logical; if TRUE, remove original columns after standardization, except that of collection codes when index_herbariorum = TRUE.


std_collection
Logical; if FALSE, the function will not standardize the collection codes according to Index Herbariorum.





Value
A fully cleaned and standardized data frame ready for downstream reconciliation, duplicate handling, and label generation.


Examples
df <- read.csv("raw_herbarium_data.csv")
df_std <- barroso_std(df,
                      colname_country = "pais",
                      colname_stateProvince = "estado",
                      rm_duplicates = TRUE)

text:
barRoso::barroso_labels()

Creates printable herbarium labels from field book data stored in a CSV-formatted file. This function is optimized for records from the USA by generating geographic maps at the county level. Scientific names are cross-referenced against the lcvplants database to update taxonomy and retrieve the correct author citation. title: std_place
text:
barRoso::std_place()


Description
Cleans and standardizes the geographic columns of a biodiversity collection dataset. This includes unifying column names and harmonizing values for continent, country, stateProvince, county, municipality, and locality. The function handles translations, synonyms, upper-case anomalies, ISO country codes, and common geographic aliases.


Details
This function is used internally by the barRoso package to support record reconciliation, duplicate detection, and label generation across different biodiversity databases. It ensures consistency of location fields by correcting common mistakes and variations. Country names are translated to English and harmonized using countrycode, and country codes like "BR" or "BRA" are converted into names. Missing countries are taken from the Brazilian state (e.g. "Bahia"), from a country name in the locality (e.g. "Manaus, Brasil"), or from other records with the same state and county. Brazilian and U.S. state abbreviations are expanded to full names. Brazilian state names written out in other ways are matched to the official names: with an "Est. do", "Estado de" or "State of" prefix (e.g. "Est. do Bahia"), without accents or in another case (e.g. "Paraiba", "PARAIBA"), and "Brasilia" for the Federal District. Missing municipalities are taken from the county. Words for municipality in county and municipality, e.g. "Manaus Mun.", "Mun. de Castelo", "Município de Mucugê" or "Arriaga Municipio", are removed, leaving just the name. Localities all in upper case get just the first letter of each word in upper case, e.g. "ESTR. UBAITUBA / MARÁU AO KM 54 ." into "Estr. Ubaituba/Maráu ao Km 54.", keeping prepositions in lowercase and road codes ("BR-316"), acronyms ("ESALQ") and compass points ("10 Km NE de") in upper case.

title: barroso_write_descriptions
text:
barRoso::barroso_write_descriptions()


Description
This function reads morphological data from an Excel spreadsheet, generates standardized species descriptions in plain text and Word document formats, and exports them to a Word (.docx) file. It handles complex morphological data structures including measurements, subterms and grouping of related characters. The function automatically detects measurement ranges and formats them with en dashes (e.g., “4.3–14.5 cm”). Optionally, it can compute and print averages for user-selected measurement columns when a species has more than a threshold number of values (see avg_cols and avg_min_n). Rare small and large values are written between parentheses, as usual in taxonomic descriptions, e.g. “(2–)6–40(–55) m” (see extremes).


Details
Measurements
Each cell of a measurement column has the measurements of one specimen. When a specimen was measured more than once (e.g. several leaves), the values are separated by a vertical bar, e.g. "4.5 | 7 | 11 | 14". The values of all specimens of a species are pooled to build its range.
Rare values are written between parentheses in two ways:
Marked in the spreadsheetValues written as in a description, e.g. "(5–)7–38(–45)" or "(2–)6 | 9 | 12", are always kept as extremes when they are beyond the range of the other values. AutomaticWith extremes = c(0.1, 0.9), when a species has at least extremes_min_n values, the range covers the values from the 10th to the 90th percentile, and the smallest and largest values outside it are written between parentheses. The range limits are always measured values. With fewer values, the range goes from the smallest to the largest value.
Counts
Columns with just numbers, e.g. LEAF SECONDARY-VENATION pairs with "6 | 8 | 12", or FLOWER STAMEN number with "10", are counts: their values are pooled into ranges, with rare values between parentheses, as the measurements. The lowercase words at the end of the column name are written after the range, e.g. “6–12 pairs”, or “fascicles 5–15 per axis” for STAMINATE-INFLORESCENCE FASCICLES per axis, except “number” and “count”, e.g. “stamen 8–10”. Write counts in their own columns, and any text in another column, e.g. “curved distally towards the marginal vein” in LEAF SECONDARY-VENATION.
Maximum values, thickness and diameter
Measurements known only by their maximum are written as "up to 5" (or "to 5") in all specimens of a species, and become e.g. “axis up to 5 cm long”. Columns of thickness and diameter, e.g. FRUIT PERICARP thickness (mm) and INFLORESCENCE CAPITULUM diameter (mm), are written as “1–2 mm thick” and “3–4 mm in diam.”.
Punctuation
Each organ (e.g. STIPULE) is a sentence. Its single traits are separated by commas, while parts with their own traits in lowercase (e.g. HABIT STEM color, LEAF PETIOLE shape) start after a semicolon, e.g. “Shrub 1.8 m tall, erect, branched; stem striated, gray, glabrous. Stipule 1 pair, lateral to petiole, 11–16 × 2–3 mm, lanceolate, base truncate, apex acute.”. A part without traits in lowercase, like STIPULE BASE, is a single trait.
Column naming conventions
The function relies on a structured column naming system to parse and organize morphological traits. Columns must follow these conventions:
Main character groupsUse ALL CAPS for the primary category: HABIT, STIPULE, LEAF, INFLORESCENCE, FLOWER, FRUIT, SEED. These will become section headers. Organs of two words are joined by a hyphen, e.g. LEAF-BLADE and STAMINATE-INFLORESCENCE for “Leaf blade” and “Staminate inflorescence”, as are terms like SECONDARY-VEINS.
Simple charactersLowercase descriptive terms after the main group. Examples: LEAF shape, LEAF margin, FLOWER symmetry. These will be appended directly after the lowercase group name.
Hierarchical charactersUse ALL CAPS for subgroup terms. Examples: LEAF PETIOLE length (cm), FLOWER SEPALS shape. The capitalized term (PETIOLE, SEPALS) is extracted once and used as a subheading, followed by its traits in the order of the columns, e.g. “stamen 10, sessile, anthers brownish, glabrous, 5–6 × 1 mm”.
MeasurementsInclude units in parentheses for automatic detection: LEAF length (cm), STIPULE width (mm), HABIT height (m). Multiple measurements (e.g., length + width) are automatically combined with “×” and the unit is placed at the end.
Column name flexibilitySpaces, dots, or underscores can be used as separators. All of the following are valid:

STIPULE length (mm)
STIPULE.length.(mm)
STIPULE_length_mm
LEAF PETIOLE shape
LEAF.PETIOLE.shape

Example dataset
The package includes an example dataset chars_dataset containing morphological data for 15 species of Ouratea (Ochnaceae) compiled from herbarium specimens and field observations for a taxonomic revision. This dataset demonstrates proper column naming conventions and can be used to test the function:
data(chars_dataset) head(names(chars_dataset))
Creating a template
To create a properly formatted Excel template with all required columns for your plant group, use the companion function barroso_chars_template. This function generates a ready-to-use template based on your species list and selected plant group (e.g., “Ochnaceae”, “Asteraceae”, “Orchidaceae”, “Leguminosae-Papilionoideae”), saving hours of manual column creation.


Create a template for Ochnaceae
barroso_chars_template( species_df = my_species_list, plant_group = “Ochnaceae”, filename = “Ochnaceae_template” )

Arguments







Argument
Description




xlsx_path
Character. Path to the .xlsx file containing morphological data with properly structured column names (see Details for naming conventions).


species_cols
Character vector or integer indices. Column names or indices used to build the species header (e.g., c(“Genus”, “Species”, “Author”) or 1:3). These can be combined flexibly (e.g., a single “Scientific_name” column or separate Genus, Species, and Author columns).


character_cols
Character vector or integer indices. Column names or indices of morphological character columns (e.g., c(“HABIT”, “LEAF shape”, “LEAF length (cm)”) or 4:20). These must follow the naming conventions described in Details.


sheet
Character string or integer. Sheet name or index passed to readxl::read_excel(). Default is 1.


species_filter
Optional character vector of species names to filter. Only species matching these names will have descriptions generated. The names should match the species name as it appears when concatenating the species_cols columns (without authorship).


avg_cols
Optional character vector or integer indices of columns for which an average should be reported, displayed immediately after the existing range (e.g. “3–8 × 1–2 cm, average 5.5 × 1.5 cm”). Must be a subset of character_cols. Default NULL (no averages reported).


avg_min_n
Integer. Minimum number of non-empty observations per species required for an average to be reported. Averages are emitted only when the number of observed values is strictly greater than avg_min_n. Default 3 (i.e., need at least 4 values for averaging).


extremes
Numeric vector of two percentiles (between 0 and 1), or NULL. Values below the first or above the second percentile of a species are written between parentheses, e.g. “(2–)6–40(–55) m”, when the species has at least extremes_min_n values. Use NULL to keep just the extremes marked in the spreadsheet. Default c(0.1, 0.9).


extremes_min_n
Integer. Minimum number of values of a species before automatic extremes are used. Default 10.


approx_char
Character string to use for approximate measurements when no variation is present (e.g., “ca.” or “c.”). Default is “ca.”. Set to NULL to disable adding approximation. Examples: "ca. 0.1 × 0.1 cm" (no variation) vs "1.3–2.5 × 0.6–1.1 cm" (variation present, no “ca.”).


font_family
Character string. Font family for the Word document. Default is “Times New Roman”. Common options include “Arial”, “Calibri”, “Cambria”.


font_size
Numeric. Font size in points. Default is 12.


species_bold
Logical. Whether to make species names bold. Default is TRUE.


species_italic
Logical. Whether to make species names italic. Default is TRUE (following botanical conventions).


group_bold
Logical. Whether to make group names (e.g., “Habit”, “Leaf”) bold. Default is TRUE.


group_italic
Logical. Whether to make group names italic. Default is FALSE.


description_bold
Logical. Whether to make description text bold. Default is FALSE.


description_italic
Logical. Whether to make description text italic. Default is FALSE.


verbose
Logical. Print progress messages. Default TRUE.


filename
Output file base name (without extension). Default NULL (uses Excel filename with “_descriptions” suffix).


dir
Output directory. Default NULL (uses Excel filename as directory name).





Value
Invisibly returns a data.frame with two columns:

species_name: Full species name with authorship
description_plain: Plain text description

The main output is a Word document (.docx) saved to the specified directory.


Examples
# Basic usage with example dataset
data(chars_dataset)

# First, save the example dataset to Excel
library(openxlsx)
write.xlsx(chars_dataset, "chars_dataset.xlsx")

# Generate descriptions using proper column selection
barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "chars_dataset.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),  # Taxonomic identification
  character_cols = 19:131,  # Morphological character columns
  approx_char = "ca."  # Add "ca." to measurements without variation
)

# Generate descriptions with average calculation
barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
  character_cols = 4:20,
  avg_cols = c("LEAF length (cm)", "FRUIT length (cm)"),
  avg_min_n = 3,  # Calculate averages when n > 3 observations
  approx_char = "ca."
)

# Filter to specific species only
barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species"),
  character_cols = 3:15,
  species_filter = c("Ouratea concinna", "Ouratea coarctata")
)

# Customize text formatting in Word output
barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = 1:3,
  character_cols = 4:25,
  font_family = "Arial",
  font_size = 11,
  species_bold = TRUE,
  species_italic = TRUE,
  group_bold = FALSE,
  group_italic = TRUE,
  description_bold = FALSE,
  description_italic = FALSE,
  filename = "MySpeciesDescriptions",
  dir = "Output"
)
